title: European Cities Deploy NVIDIA-Powered AI Agents to Run Smarter Urban Operations
text: Keeping a city running means making decisions that affect residents every day — from when to repair a road to how to use energy more efficiently. Across the EMEA region, cities and local software, infrastructure and integration partners are using NVIDIA accelerated computing to build physical AI agents and digital twins that help teams make those decisions. These applications can anticipate maintenance needs, guide urban planning and make public services more responsive. Software partners including ABA Technology , Akila , Galene AI , Honeywell Technologies , K2K , Linker Vision , Milestone , Onetera , ThinkDeep and Younite AI are using NVIDIA physical and agentic AI to develop solutions for city operations and public services. https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/linker-vision.mp4 Video courtesy of Linker Vision and MVRDV. NVIDIA Cosmos open models and the NVIDIA Metropolis Blueprint for video search and summarization (VSS) help agents interpret video and identify conditions, such as traffic congestion, equipment condition, underused spaces and safety hazards, that need attention. NVIDIA Nemotron open models enable developers to build agents that reason over information, respond in natural language and deploy digital twins with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. Projects span Belgium, Finland, France, Italy, the Netherlands, Poland, Sweden, the U.K. and elsewhere. Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements In the U.K., the Liverpool City Region , K2K is exploring how to build AI factories using NVIDIA accelerated computing, Cosmos and the VSS blueprint that can support urban planning and public services — testing applications for mobility and safety. The Island of Jersey is working with K2K to strengthen decision-making, mobility and urban planning while advancing clean energy and public services. Innovation City Belfast is exploring a pilot with K2K focused on smart mobility, transport systems, citizen safety and event and response management. https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/IKM®-�-Video-GTC-V.10.10.2-compressed.mp4 Video courtesy of K2K. In France, the Department of Côte-d’Or , Akila and ThinkDeep built operations agents that combine sensor, infrastructure and historical data in a sovereign digital twin using NVIDIA Nemotron, Omniverse and accelerated computing, with Cosmos adoption planned for video data. Across more than 500 public buildings, the agents support energy, compliance, safety and climate resilience, and cut document search time from weeks to minutes and reduce total operating costs by 10%, targeting 30% at scale. https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Akila-CGCO-compressed.mp4 Video courtesy of Akila. In addition, Port Sud de France in Sète is working with ThinkDeep’s agentic platform that uses Cosmos and Nemotron to analyze cargo and safety data, coordinate operations and guide secure handling of hazardous materials. In Italy’s Milan region, Galene.AI , Dell Technologies and TD Synnex are deploying an NVIDIA-powered, locally operated AI factory, starting with Cinisello Balsamo and planning expansion to four additional municipalities. Services include real-time translation, citizen chatbots and assistance with procurement and funding. These applications aim to simplify administrative work and help people get access to municipal data in seconds versus hours, while keeping local governance of data. At Belgium’s Port of Antwerp-Bruges , Milestone and Dell Technologies are testing how agentic vision AI technologies, using NVIDIA Cosmos and the VSS blueprint, could support complex use cases such as oil-spill warnings by training models with synthetic data to prepare for incidents where real-world data is scarce. In the Nordics, Younite AI is developing a digital twin experience with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries for Gothenburg in Sweden as a part of the EU’s Citiverse initiative, focused on helping cities simulate changes and improve accessibility by providing event entrance previews, seating and crowd conditions before arrival. These cities point toward a broader ambition: adapting agentic applications to local needs and extending them across departments and neighboring municipalities and countries such as Poland’s city of Wroclaw. Elsewhere in the region, Honeywell Technologies is deploying Forge Cognition, powered by NVIDIA Nemotron, Cosmos, Omniverse and the VSS blueprint, at the Dubai Fairmont Hotel to connect AI agents with building systems and improve reliability, energy efficiency and operations. https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/honeywell.mp4 Video courtesy of Honeywell Technologies. Building the AI Infrastructure for European Cities For European cities, scaling from pilots to everyday operations requires infrastructure that can process local data, customize models and run AI agents. System builders and infrastructure partners including Cisco , Dell Technologies , HPE , Lenovo and Supermicro are packaging NVIDIA accelerated computing, networking and storage into locally operated AI factories. These systems let cities customize and run intelligent applications locally while retaining control of their data, models and operations. Nebius, Nscale and Net Zero Compute are part of the broader ecosystem building AI factories designed to accelerate deployment and reduce costs for agentic services. EY and Accenture provide the integration and operational expertise to connect applications with city systems. Their work helps cities build repeatable deployment blueprints that they can adapt across departments and expand as local needs grow. Learn how NVIDIA and its ecosystem are bringing physical AI, agentic AI and local AI factories to cities worldwide at Smart City Expo World Congress , running Nov. 3-5 in Barcelona. title: All Systems Go: Global PC App Ecosystem Ready for NVIDIA RTX Spark
text: NVIDIA RTX Spark is a new beginning for the PC — a reinvention combining the capabilities of a gaming PC, a creative studio and a personal AI supercomputer into a single superchip. With up to 128GB of unified memory and 1 petaflop of AI compute, RTX Spark delivers the full stack of NVIDIA RTX and CUDA technologies for creators, developers and gamers, while unlocking a new paradigm in personal computing via powerful local AI agents. Last week, NVIDIA and Microsoft announced that RTX Spark laptops will be available on Friday, Oct. 16 . Ahead of the launch, NVIDIA and its ecosystem partners are rolling out new software features and performance optimizations to expand what’s possible with local AI on RTX Spark. New and upcoming RTX Spark updates — among the thousands of apps, games and models available at launch — include: New agent features, models and tools that enhance local agents on RTX Spark: Updates to top agent apps including GitHub Copilot, Hermes, OpenClaw, Perplexity, Pi and WorkBuddy streamline setup on RTX Spark, improve security with OpenShell and Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC), and enable hybrid local and cloud AI routing. The NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B model, purpose-built for agentic AI on RTX Spark, releases on Thursday, Oct. 15. NVIDIA PAIR moves out of beta and adds llama.cpp support. Top creative apps optimized for RTX Spark: Up to 2x performance is coming soon to Adobe’s top apps. NVIDIA and Adobe have collaborated to rearchitect Photoshop for GPU-accelerated compositing and Premiere for playback, rendering, effects and more. The NVIDIA Broadcast 2.3 release brings new Video Super Resolution, Video Frame Generation, offline file processing and agent Model Context Protocol (MCP) controls to the app. NVIDIA RTX Video Frame Generation and high dynamic range (HDR) capabilities are available now in ComfyUI to accelerate AI generative video workflows. NVIDIA DLSS Ray Reconstruction will be available in Blender 5.3 in November to improve interactivity in the viewport. Developer tools are now ready for RTX Spark: Top developer frameworks are now available for RTX Spark, including PyTorch, Python and CUDA, as well as all CUDA libraries. GitHub Copilot, Pi and other coding agents are now optimized for RTX Spark. Llama.cpp adds support for decision models, and releases a Windows app. Hundreds of top games and anti-cheat are supported on RTX Spark, plus: A 2x faster DLSS 5 AI model arrives Friday, Oct. 16, and a new Performance Mode for DLSS Frame Generation is available today via the NVIDIA App beta . Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, the third-generation small language model (SLM) for NVIDIA ACE AI game characters, releases Friday, Oct. 23. The latest RTX Remix update, including DLSS 5 support, releases on Friday, Oct. 23. Advancing Local AI Agents With New Apps, Models and Tools AI is changing the way people interact with PCs. Agent popularity skyrocketed this year, with projects such as OpenClaw and Hermes topping popularity charts on GitHub. Local large language models (LLMs) surpassed the intelligence threshold to power agents, with models like Qwen 3.8-Flash-Next catching up to frontier cloud models released just a few months ago. As a result, local LLM downloads are already 5x higher than all of last year. From models to agent harnesses to security to tools, NVIDIA is partnering closely with the local AI ecosystem to make RTX Spark the ideal hardware to run local agents. Local AI Agents Made Easy On RTX Spark From the first boot of RTX Spark, users will be greeted with a “Getting Started” screen to choose and install their agent app. These agents will come with new, secure sandboxing technology thanks to NVIDIA OpenShell and MXC. MXC delivers operating system-level security, while OpenShell makes it simpler for agents to adopt MXC and adds advanced capabilities such as credential protection and security monitoring. Hermes Agent will integrate granular OpenShell controls and MXC by the end of the month. OpenClaw and GitHub Copilot now support MXC. After installing an agent, setting up local AI is also now seamless in GitHub Copilot, Hermes Agent, OpenClaw, Perplexity, Pi and WorkBuddy. The apps will recommend an optimized local model and settings configuration for RTX Spark, and set it all up for users in a few clicks. Many users want the best of both worlds — local models for free iteration, and cloud models for frontier intelligence. NVIDIA Switchyard, an open source model router library, enables agents to intelligently route queries between local and cloud LLMs, allowing the user to minimize cloud usage but still obtain similar results to just running on cloud. Hermes will be adding Switchyard later in October, and other agents like Perplexity Computer and GitHub Copilot have integrated their own routing solutions. Software providers have made it simple for agents to connect to top Windows apps, with easy-to-use MCP libraries and command line interfaces (CLIs). NVIDIA has also now made available MCPs for its applications, including NVIDIA App, Broadcast, PAIR, Omniverse, RTX Remix and a large library of CUDA-X Skills . NVIDIA is also releasing AI playbooks for RTX Spark, available on Friday, Oct 16. Users can set up their first agent, build an AI chief of staff, configure their system for development or design a creative assistant. Meet Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B: Built for Local Agents on RTX Spark NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB, available Thursday, Oct. 15, is a new LLM purpose-built for running local agents on RTX Spark. This model is a 74B parameter, 9B-active-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, packed into 24GB using 2-bit quantization with advanced quantization-aware training techniques to retain quality. It aims to achieve the optimal balance between speed and intelligence, being faster than most popular dense models while smarter than most popular MoE models with a similar memory footprint. Users will be able to run Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B at launch through llama.cpp, vLLM, Ollama, Unsloth and LM Studio. It will also be directly accessible via agents such as Hermes and OpenClaw. Like other Nemotron models, Bolt 74B is fully open source — including training data, weights and recipes — so developers can fine-tune and customize their own agents. The Perfect PAIR Local AI doesn’t have to run on just one PC. NVIDIA PAIR , a personal AI router, is officially moving out of beta today, making it easier to tap into the total AI compute of compatible PCs on a local network. The free, open source software tool automatically discovers and connects devices, installs AI models and inference engines, and distributes AI workloads across available systems. The official release adds llama.cpp support, direct model downloads from Hugging Face, customizable inference engine settings and RTX Spark support, along with a variety of inference and user experience improvements. PAIR works on Windows, Linux and macOS. Developers can contribute to the open source project via Github — just one month after the initial PAIR release, the community has already contributed over 10 features and fixes to the release. Sparking Creativity RTX Spark brings over 130 accelerated apps, CUDA for fast video and image generation, and RTX technologies such as DLSS, NVENC and OptiX to advanced content creation workflows — all in a thin and light laptop with on-the-go performance. Adobe Accelerates Creative Applications for RTX Spark Adobe is optimizing its industry-leading creative applications, including Photoshop, Premiere and Substance 3D, for RTX Spark, delivering up to 2x faster AI, editing, color and effects across creative workflows. In Photoshop, GPU-accelerated compositing makes complex image editing faster and more responsive, with improvements to the Remove Tool and effects such as Light Leaks. Premiere accelerates demanding video editing tasks, including playback, rendering, color grading and AI-powered features such as Enhance Speech and Object Mask. Meanwhile, Substance 3D Painter speeds up texture creation workflows, from baking high-resolution mesh maps to opening, saving and exporting large projects. The updates will be rolling out in phases, with AI feature optimizations in Photoshop and Premiere now ready in beta, and with Adobe Substance 3D updates coming soon. Opt in to the beta to get access to the RTX Spark-optimized builds. Latest NVIDIA Broadcast Brings New AI Effects to Live and Recorded Content Available for download now, NVIDIA Broadcast 2.3 runs natively on RTX Spark, and adds new RTX Video Super Resolution and Frame Generation AI effects and Studio Voice profiles. A new Offline File Processor lets creators apply Broadcast effects to prerecorded content, with many effects running at higher quality since there isn’t a need to maintain real-time performance. The update also introduces a new MCP server and skill that lets local AI agents adjust effects, change settings and process files directly through the Broadcast app. RTX Video Brings Frame Generation and HDR to ComfyUI ComfyUI is expanding its RTX Video tools with two new nodes: RTX Video Frame Generation and RTX Video HDR. It’s also providing the ability to export EXR files, giving creators more ways to enhance AI-generated video. https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/comfyui_nvidia_vfx_nodes_explainer_4k48_v4.mp4 RTX Video Frame Generation increases video frame rates for smoother motion for GeForce RTX 40 Series GPUs and newer, while RTX Video HDR converts standard dynamic range (SDR) footage to HDR for greater flexibility in color grading. Combined with RTX Video Super Resolution, these tools enable creators to upscale, enhance and refine video within a single ComfyUI workflow. For example, creators can combine LTX 2.5 with RTX Video Frame Generation and HDR to transform a 1080p, 30 frames-per-second (fps) SDR clip into a smoother 60 fps HDR video exported as EXR files ready for color grading. Blender Adds DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction Blender has released a beta version of its popular 3D editor, adding compatibility for RTX Spark. Download Blender version 5.3 to get access. Coming next month, Blender will also be adding support for DLSS Ray Reconstruction, allowing for real-time updates in the viewport so artists can navigate a scene while previewing it in real time. Code, Test and Deploy From RTX Spark Developers are moving from writing code to directing AI agents. This new development paradigm is requiring many to spread their work across their laptop, a cloud LLM and a cloud virtual machine, where they test and prototype. RTX Spark enables developers to work on one machine, running all their workloads and libraries, testing and prototyping, and deploying. They can now do so directly in Windows with the new Windows Developer Config, which enhances the user experience for devs and installs all the top developer tools — or via Windows Subsystem for Linux, where they can get access to the same packages they’ll use to publish to the cloud. Developer Tools Are RTX-Spark Ready NVIDIA has partnered with Microsoft to ensure that developer tools are ready for RTX Spark. Alongside RTX Spark, the community is releasing: The first PyTorch-CUDA build for Windows on Arm. The first Python build that is native by default on Windows on Arm, with Python 3.15. The first native Conda installer for Windows on Arm, with over 2,000 Conda packages. 97% of the top 15,000 Python wheels are ready, thanks to work with the ecosystem. NVIDIA will be working closely with the community to ready the remaining wheels. Development is now mostly done by agents. NVIDIA Skills — an open source GitHub repository that teaches agents how to use NVIDIA CUDA-X tools and libraries — lets users develop apps that are accelerated on NVIDIA technologies, even without knowing anything about CUDA. Coding Agents Are Ready for Local AI In addition to GitHub Copilot — one of the most popular coding agents, used by millions worldwide — adding support for MXC, it’s updating its model router HydraFusion with support for local models. This enables developers to use their local hardware to reduce token consumption while tapping into frontier intelligence. NVIDIA RTX Spark is a new beginning for the PC — a reinvention combining the capabilities of a gaming PC, a creative studio and a personal AI supercomputer into a single superchip. With up to 128GB of unified memory and 1 petaflop of AI compute, RTX Spark delivers the full stack of NVIDIA RTX and CUDA technologies for creators, developers and gamers, while unlocking a new paradigm in personal computing via powerful local AI agents.

Last week, NVIDIA and Microsoft announced that RTX Spark laptops will be available on Friday, Oct. 16. Ahead of the launch, NVIDIA and its ecosystem partners are rolling out new software features and performance optimizations to expand what’s possible with local AI on RTX Spark. 

New and upcoming RTX Spark updates — among the thousands of apps, games and models available at launch — include: 

  • New agent features, models and tools that enhance local agents on RTX Spark: 
    • Updates to top agent apps including GitHub Copilot, Hermes, OpenClaw, Perplexity, Pi and WorkBuddy streamline setup on RTX Spark, improve security with OpenShell and Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC), and enable hybrid local and cloud AI routing.
    • The NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B model, purpose-built for agentic AI on RTX Spark, releases on Thursday, Oct. 15. 
    • NVIDIA PAIR moves out of beta and adds llama.cpp support.
  • Top creative apps optimized for RTX Spark:
    • Up to 2x performance is coming soon to Adobe’s top apps. NVIDIA and Adobe have collaborated to rearchitect Photoshop for GPU-accelerated compositing and Premiere for playback, rendering, effects and more.
    • The NVIDIA Broadcast 2.3 release brings new Video Super Resolution, Video Frame Generation, offline file processing and agent Model Context Protocol (MCP) controls to the app.
    • NVIDIA RTX Video Frame Generation and high dynamic range (HDR) capabilities are available now in ComfyUI to accelerate AI generative video workflows.
    • NVIDIA DLSS Ray Reconstruction will be available in Blender 5.3 in November to improve interactivity in the viewport.
  • Developer tools are now ready for RTX Spark:
    • Top developer frameworks are now available for RTX Spark, including PyTorch, Python and CUDA, as well as all CUDA libraries. 
    • GitHub Copilot, Pi and other coding agents are now optimized for RTX Spark.
    • Llama.cpp adds support for decision models, and releases a Windows app.
  • Hundreds of top games and anti-cheat are supported on RTX Spark, plus:
    • A 2x faster DLSS 5 AI model arrives Friday, Oct. 16, and a new Performance Mode for DLSS Frame Generation is available today via the NVIDIA App beta.
    • Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, the third-generation small language model (SLM) for NVIDIA ACE AI game characters, releases Friday, Oct. 23.
    • The latest RTX Remix update, including DLSS 5 support, releases on Friday, Oct. 23.

Advancing Local AI Agents With New Apps, Models and Tools

AI is changing the way people interact with PCs. Agent popularity skyrocketed this year, with projects such as OpenClaw and Hermes topping popularity charts on GitHub. Local large language models (LLMs) surpassed the intelligence threshold to power agents, with models like Qwen 3.8-Flash-Next catching up to frontier cloud models released just a few months ago. As a result, local LLM downloads are already 5x higher than all of last year.

From models to agent harnesses to security to tools, NVIDIA is partnering closely with the local AI ecosystem to make RTX Spark the ideal hardware to run local agents. 

Local AI Agents Made Easy On RTX Spark

From the first boot of RTX Spark, users will be greeted with a “Getting Started” screen to choose and install their agent app.

These agents will come with new, secure sandboxing technology thanks to NVIDIA OpenShell and MXC. MXC delivers operating system-level security, while OpenShell makes it simpler for agents to adopt MXC and adds advanced capabilities such as credential protection and security monitoring. Hermes Agent will integrate granular OpenShell controls and MXC by the end of the month. OpenClaw and GitHub Copilot now support MXC.

After installing an agent, setting up local AI is also now seamless in GitHub Copilot, Hermes Agent, OpenClaw, Perplexity, Pi and WorkBuddy. The apps will recommend an optimized local model and settings configuration for RTX Spark, and set it all up for users in a few clicks.

Many users want the best of both worlds — local models for free iteration, and cloud models for frontier intelligence. NVIDIA Switchyard, an open source model router library, enables agents to intelligently route queries between local and cloud LLMs, allowing the user to minimize cloud usage but still obtain similar results to just running on cloud. Hermes will be adding Switchyard later in October, and other agents like Perplexity Computer and GitHub Copilot have integrated their own routing solutions.

Software providers have made it simple for agents to connect to top Windows apps, with easy-to-use MCP libraries and command line interfaces (CLIs). NVIDIA has also now made available MCPs for its applications, including NVIDIA App, Broadcast, PAIR, Omniverse, RTX Remix and a large library of CUDA-X Skills. 

NVIDIA is also releasing AI playbooks for RTX Spark, available on Friday, Oct 16. Users can set up their first agent, build an AI chief of staff, configure their system for development or design a creative assistant.

Meet Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B: Built for Local Agents on RTX Spark

NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB, available Thursday, Oct. 15, is a new LLM purpose-built for running local agents on RTX Spark. 

This model is a 74B parameter, 9B-active-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, packed into 24GB using 2-bit quantization with advanced quantization-aware training techniques to retain quality. It aims to achieve the optimal balance between speed and intelligence, being faster than most popular dense models while smarter than most popular MoE models with a similar memory footprint.

Users will be able to run Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B at launch through llama.cpp, vLLM, Ollama, Unsloth and LM Studio. It will also be directly accessible via agents such as Hermes and OpenClaw.  

Like other Nemotron models, Bolt 74B is fully open source — including training data, weights and recipes — so developers can fine-tune and customize their own agents.

The Perfect PAIR

Local AI doesn’t have to run on just one PC. NVIDIA PAIR, a personal AI router, is officially moving out of beta today, making it easier to tap into the total AI compute of compatible PCs on a local network. The free, open source software tool automatically discovers and connects devices, installs AI models and inference engines, and distributes AI workloads across available systems.

The official release adds llama.cpp support, direct model downloads from Hugging Face, customizable inference engine settings and RTX Spark support, along with a variety of inference and user experience improvements. 

PAIR works on Windows, Linux and macOS. Developers can contribute to the open source project via Github — just one month after the initial PAIR release, the community has already contributed over 10 features and fixes to the release. 

Sparking Creativity

RTX Spark brings over 130 accelerated apps, CUDA for fast video and image generation, and RTX technologies such as DLSS, NVENC and OptiX to advanced content creation workflows — all in a thin and light laptop with on-the-go performance.

Adobe Accelerates Creative Applications for RTX Spark

Adobe is optimizing its industry-leading creative applications, including Photoshop, Premiere and Substance 3D, for RTX Spark, delivering up to 2x faster AI, editing, color and effects across creative workflows. 

In Photoshop, GPU-accelerated compositing makes complex image editing faster and more responsive, with improvements to the Remove Tool and effects such as Light Leaks. Premiere accelerates demanding video editing tasks, including playback, rendering, color grading and AI-powered features such as Enhance Speech and Object Mask. Meanwhile, Substance 3D Painter speeds up texture creation workflows, from baking high-resolution mesh maps to opening, saving and exporting large projects.

The updates will be rolling out in phases, with AI feature optimizations in Photoshop and Premiere now ready in beta, and with Adobe Substance 3D updates coming soon. Opt in to the beta to get access to the RTX Spark-optimized builds. 

Latest NVIDIA Broadcast Brings New AI Effects to Live and Recorded Content

Available for download now, NVIDIA Broadcast 2.3 runs natively on RTX Spark, and adds new RTX Video Super Resolution and Frame Generation AI effects and Studio Voice profiles.

A new Offline File Processor lets creators apply Broadcast effects to prerecorded content, with many effects running at higher quality since there isn’t a need to maintain real-time performance. The update also introduces a new MCP server and skill that lets local AI agents adjust effects, change settings and process files directly through the Broadcast app.

RTX Video Brings Frame Generation and HDR to ComfyUI

ComfyUI is expanding its RTX Video tools with two new nodes: RTX Video Frame Generation and RTX Video HDR. It’s also providing the ability to export EXR files, giving creators more ways to enhance AI-generated video.

 

RTX Video Frame Generation increases video frame rates for smoother motion for GeForce RTX 40 Series GPUs and newer, while RTX Video HDR converts standard dynamic range (SDR) footage to HDR for greater flexibility in color grading. Combined with RTX Video Super Resolution, these tools enable creators to upscale, enhance and refine video within a single ComfyUI workflow.

For example, creators can combine LTX 2.5 with RTX Video Frame Generation and HDR to transform a 1080p, 30 frames-per-second (fps) SDR clip into a smoother 60 fps HDR video exported as EXR files ready for color grading. 

Blender Adds DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction

Blender has released a beta version of its popular 3D editor, adding compatibility for RTX Spark. Download Blender version 5.3 to get access.

Coming next month, Blender will also be adding support for DLSS Ray Reconstruction, allowing for real-time updates in the viewport so artists can navigate a scene while previewing it in real time. 

Code, Test and Deploy From RTX Spark

Developers are moving from writing code to directing AI agents. This new development paradigm is requiring many to spread their work across their laptop, a cloud LLM and a cloud virtual machine, where they test and prototype. 

RTX Spark enables developers to work on one machine, running all their workloads and libraries, testing and prototyping, and deploying. They can now do so directly in Windows with the new Windows Developer Config, which enhances the user experience for devs and installs all the top developer tools — or via Windows Subsystem for Linux, where they can get access to the same packages they’ll use to publish to the cloud.

Developer Tools Are RTX-Spark Ready

NVIDIA has partnered with Microsoft to ensure that developer tools are ready for RTX Spark. Alongside RTX Spark, the community is releasing:

  • The first PyTorch-CUDA build for Windows on Arm.
  • The first Python build that is native by default on Windows on Arm, with Python 3.15.
  • The first native Conda installer for Windows on Arm, with over 2,000 Conda packages.
  • 97% of the top 15,000 Python wheels are ready, thanks to work with the ecosystem. NVIDIA will be working closely with the community to ready the remaining wheels.

Development is now mostly done by agents. NVIDIA Skills — an open source GitHub repository that teaches agents how to use NVIDIA CUDA-X tools and libraries — lets users develop apps that are accelerated on NVIDIA technologies, even without knowing anything about CUDA.

Coding Agents Are Ready for Local AI

In addition to GitHub Copilot — one of the most popular coding agents, used by millions worldwide — adding support for MXC, it’s updating its model router HydraFusion with support for local models. This enables developers to use their local hardware to reduce token consumption while tapping into frontier intelligence.

Microsoft is making coding models, such as MAI 1.1 Coding Flash, available locally, and adding llama.cpp as a backend to Windows ML — extending the supported models and enabling the latest NVIDIA performance optimizations.

Get started with GitHub Copilot running locally when RTX Spark launches.

Llama.cpp Adds Support for Decision Models, Releases a Windows App

Decision models are the latest breakthrough in AI development. They give AI agents a near-instant way to make decisions, without lengthy reasoning loops. They can choose what to do next, from classifying requests to selecting the next action, up to 200x faster than traditional agents. Decision models are now supported in llama.cpp and Unsloth on RTX Spark and GeForce RTX GPUs.

Llama.cpp is also releasing today Llama Windows, a Windows-native companion app for llama.cpp, enabling an easy-to-use user interface to download and run models locally, without having to go into the command line. This app, like llama.cpp, is optimized for RTX Spark. Learn more on the Hugging Face blog.

Game On: RTX Spark Launches With Hundreds of Top Games and DLSS 5

RTX Spark is ready for gaming, with hundreds of top titles available when laptops launch on Friday, Oct. 16, including CONTROL Resonant, Cyberpunk 2077, Fortnite, Gears of War: E-Day, Genshin Impact, Hogwarts Legacy, Honkai: Star Rail, Marvel Rivals, NARAKA: BLADEPOINT, NBA 2K27, World of Warcraft and many more.

NVIDIA has worked to bring the full stack of RTX technologies, including DLSS, Reflex, Remix, G-SYNC and ray tracing, to the new platform, along with collaborating with game developers to enable anti-cheat support for popular multiplayer games. Learn more about gaming on RTX Spark. 

DLSS 5 Brings Neural Rendering to RTX Spark

NVIDIA DLSS 5 with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering is also coming to RTX Spark on launch day. The technology uses AI to enhance lighting and materials with lifelike detail, making game worlds and characters more realistic while preserving developers’ artistic vision. A new, 2x faster DLSS 5 AI model debuts in NBA 2K27 on Friday, Oct. 16, boosting frame rates by up to 1.4x. The faster model will also power DLSS 5 in Hogwarts Legacy starting Thursday, Nov. 5, and Where Winds Meet in late November.

DLSS 5 is also coming to NVIDIA RTX Remix on Friday, Oct. 23, so modders can add better materials, lighting and shadows to classic characters and environments, as shown from modder Sparkles/Kim2091 in her in-development project, Fallout 4 RTX.

Read more about DLSS 5 on RTX Spark on GeForce.com.

Game Agents Running Locally on RTX Spark

Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB is the third-generation SLM for NVIDIA ACE, the suite of technologies for building in-game AI agents that deliver next-generation gaming experiences. The first-generation model was in a public beta earlier this year for PUBG, allowing players to team up with AI teammates, while the more efficient second-generation model previewed in Aniimo at Gamescom, turning standard creatures into voice-responsive companions.

Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B combines natural conversation with multi-turn tool use, instruction following and grounding in application state to power fast local voice and device assistants, interactive characters and embedded interfaces.

Designed for a low memory footprint and fast time to first token, this model enables responsive local experiences while leaving headroom for applications and other AI models. Its new conversational mode helps keep responses concise and speech-ready, and developers can turn reasoning on or off as needed. 

Starting Friday, Oct. 23, test drive the third-generation Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB inside SkyrimNET, an AI nonplayable character (NPC) modding platform by MinLL for The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim. SkyrimNET transforms every NPC into an unscripted, interactive character equipped with personal memory, voice and autonomy for dynamic conversations and context-aware quests generated on the fly.

Now compatible with RTX Spark, SkyrimNET supports both cloud and local inference across multiple models, with the latest Nemotron models delivering best-in-class performance for efficient and fast in-game interactions. Download the build on GitHub.

Accelerating Modding Workflows in RTX Remix

As AI agents continue to help modders make their favorite classic games compatible with the RTX Remix renderer, NVIDIA is streamlining asset updates with a major overhaul to its AI-powered texture generation workflow. Launching Friday, Oct. 23, as part of Remix 1.6, ComfyUI Version 2 replaces complex REST application programming interface (API) node connections with a dedicated AI tools layout directly in the sidebar.

This update allows modders and artists to generate physically based rendering materials natively inside RTX Remix with zero API setup required. A new batch processing feature makes it easy to scale beyond single-texture experimentation to full modding projects, while an intuitive presets system lets non-technical creators adjust key settings without touching the node graph.

title: NVIDIA Announces New Investments in France’s Startups
text: Companies in France are deploying agentic computing across industries spanning space, financial services, the public sector and scientific research, demonstrating how the country’s ecosystem has moved from ambition to application. France’s progress sits on deliberate groundwork. The AI Action Summit in February 2025 and Choose France Summits in 2025 and 2026 anchored major compute commitments on French soil. What the ecosystem has built since then spans the full stack. Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements NVIDIA’s Investments in France NVIDIA has been investing in France’s startup ecosystem, having previously invested in leading technology companies including Alice&Bob, Gradium and Scintil Photonics . Across all of Europe, NVIDIA has committed nearly $10 billion to the technology ecosystem. Today, NVIDIA announced new planned investments in Doctolib, Entalpic , Genesis AI and Pigment . These startups are innovating to solve challenges across healthcare, materials discovery, physical AI and business planning. Doctolib , a European healthcare technology company, builds agents that free up healthcare professionals to deliver better care, while providing patients with a digital health companion that improves access to care and supports more preventive, continuous medicine. Entalpic , a Paris-based startup, accelerates the engineering of advanced materials at the atomic scale, with particular expertise in surfaces and interfaces for semiconductor manufacturing and next-generation electronics. Genesis AI is a global robotics company developing general-purpose robots with frontier intelligence and capabilities through its foundation models, data collection systems, simulation infrastructure and robot hardware. Pigment , a Paris-based enterprise software company, builds a planning platform that helps businesses forecast performance, model scenarios and make decisions across finance, sales, workforce and operations. Sovereign AI Infrastructure France-based companies are expanding agentic infrastructure on NVIDIA technology. Bull is extending its European AI server production to NVIDIA Vera Rubin Ultra NVL72 systems, planned for 2028, with trays produced in Europe and rack integration at its Angers factory — inaugurated Friday, Oct. 2. Altair-1, the first satellite in a $1 billion, 50-satellite constellation with on-board autonomous capabilities, launched this month and has successfully reached orbit. Integrated by Loft Orbital and built in Abu Dhabi by Orbitworks , a joint venture between Loft Orbital and Marlan Space , the satellite is flying NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin edge modules, running Mistral’s models, for real-time Earth observation and autonomous operations in orbit. Open Models NVIDIA Nemotron open models are in production across French organizations that require sovereign, trustworthy data. LINAGORA and Docaposte have secured the CANUT framework agreement , making Twake.ai, built on NVIDIA Nemotron, the sole referenced sovereign digital workplace for more than 2,500 French public organizations. In financial services, SBS is launching a sovereign platform enabling banks to deploy governed generative and agentic services within their own environments, in collaboration with NVIDIA. Dassault Systèmes is using NVIDIA Nemotron open models and accelerated computing to advance its sovereign Industrial AI architecture, accelerating the training of its own Industry World Models and the development of its agentic Virtual Companions platform, grounded in science, physics and engineering for trusted industrial applications. Last week, Mistral introduced under private preview Mistral Large 4 open model, with state-of-the-art, open weight performance in cyber defense, manufacturing, finance and multimodal tasks, and a solid foundation for customizing models across key industries. Fondation Inria , with NVIDIA’s support, is launching a working group on open source advanced modeling and tool adoption, with findings to come in the spring of next year. Agents at Work Across Industries Across retail, public services, telecommunications and science, the pattern is consistent: open models and NVIDIA infrastructure are driving results in France. L’Oréal is integrating NVIDIA ALCHEMI into its research workflows so scientists can explore formulation possibilities in silico and better help guide laboratory research. Combining computational predictions with hands-on experimentation can make the discovery process up to 100x faster than traditional methods and maximize the potential of the group’s proprietary active ingredients. Mirakl has onboarded more than 70 million products with fine-tuned and open models running on NVIDIA GPUs and inference software, cutting seller catalog onboarding to under two hours. Photoroom and Vestiaire Collective a re demonstrating the measurable business impact of advanced visual modeling on marketplace performance. Omi helps brands bring accurate products into AI-generated marketing visuals at scale, combining its approved 3D digital twins with open models optimized on NVIDIA for 4x faster inference. In Côte-d’Or, ThinkDeep and Akila built a digital-twin agent — powered by NVIDIA Cosmos open world models, Nemotron and Omniverse libraries — managing nearly 5,800 kilometers of roads and buildings, cutting total operating costs by 10% and targeting 30% as deployment progresses. Port Sud de France runs goods processing and port security on ThinkDeep’s DeepBrain platform powered by Nemotron and Cosmos. Enchanted Tools, a robotics company headquartered in Paris, is deploying social robots to support patients in healthcare settings including pediatric cancer care. In telecom, Bouygues Telecom and Prisme.ai have launched AI Studio V2, powered by NVIDIA full-stack infrastructure, to offer all of its employees the ability to build their own agents, securely and in a controlled environment In quantum, Alice & Bob has integrated the NVIDIA NVQLink platform for its superconducting cat qubits, showing how GPUs can make quantum error correction more efficient, including for faster qubit modalities. Quandela has also been using NVQLink to build an integration between a DGX Spark system and its photonic qubits — advancing QPU-GPU supercomputing and exploring hybrid quantum-classical applications. Tune in to NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang’s GTC Berlin keynote on Wednesday, Oct. 21, at 11 a.m. CEST. Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements

The Open Data Center Specification v0.7 defines a unified blueprint for next-generation AI factory facility design — from power architecture to cooling infrastructure to physical layout. The OCP Grid Resilience Specification , published by Google , Meta, Microsoft and NVIDIA, establishes how large-scale AI infrastructure should behave during utility grid disturbances: staying connected, responding automatically and restoring to near-full load within less than two seconds. With these standards now open, manufacturers around the world have a common target to build for. Equipment makers, colocation providers and data center operators can begin designing, fabricating and delivering the infrastructure layer that powers AI factories under construction globally — without waiting for proprietary specifications from individual customers. Being NVIDIA DSX reference design -compatible, these specifications provide a validated, deployable implementation of both specs, from facility layout and power architecture to the software that monitors and responds to grid signals in real time. The design addresses a growing industry challenge. As AI training, inference and reasoning workloads expand, rack power densities continue to rise. Traditional low-voltage power distribution becomes increasingly difficult to scale, requiring more copper, more cabling and more power-conversion equipment. By adopting NVIDIA’s 800 VDC architecture, K-1 creates a path toward higher-density AI infrastructure while preserving flexibility for existing deployments. Rather than requiring a complete transition on day one, the platform is designed to phase in 800 VDC distribution where it delivers the greatest benefit, helping operators prepare for future generations of accelerated computing without extensive facility redesign. The architecture is designed around cluster-level power centers that centralize AC-to-DC conversion and distribute 800 VDC closer to compute resources. The approach simplifies downstream power delivery, supports modular expansion and creates repeatable building blocks for future AI factory growth. K-1 also reflects the system-level design philosophy behind NVIDIA AI factories, where power, cooling and computing are engineered together. With support for liquid-cooled infrastructure, scalable power distribution and future Vera Rubin-class deployments, the project demonstrates how ecosystem partners are translating NVIDIA’s AI factory architecture into deployable infrastructure designed for the next era of accelerated computing. Spectrum-6 delivers twice the switching capacity and per-lane bandwidth of Spectrum-4, and provides a lossless Ethernet AI fabric at 200G per lane, with high effective bandwidth and performance isolation that keeps one job’s traffic from slowing another’s. Meta’s Spectrum-6-based switch, N-IceCube, slots into IcePack, Meta’s 100T, liquid-cooled rack. N-IceCube runs the Facebook Open Switching System (FBOSS), Meta’s open source network operating system that contributed to OCP to support efficient networking at hyperscale. FBOSS is built on the Switch Abstraction Interface, an OCP standard NVIDIA helped develop, providing a vendor-independent way of controlling switch hardware. The announcement marks the next step in a collaboration that combines Meta’s experience operating AI infrastructure at hyperscale with NVIDIA’s networking technology. At the heart of this collaboration is Spectrum-X Multiplane technology, enabled by Spectrum-6 switches and ConnectX-9 SuperNICs. Multiplane distributes GPU traffic in hardware across up to eight independent network planes, enabling AI factories to scale beyond 100,000 GPUs with fewer switch tiers and lower infrastructure costs. Multiple paths between GPUs improve network utilization and resilience: when a component fails, traffic shifts to the remaining planes, keeping GPUs productive and AI applications running, even at reduced bandwidth. Meta and NVIDIA worked together to strengthen that resilience through deployment experience and rapid engineering iteration. The teams validated improvements across on-premises and cloud environments. “We are excited about our close partnership with NVIDIA in making multiplane fabrics operationally scalable and performant, a critical requirement both for our own infrastructure builds and for our joint cloud partners,” said Omar Baldonado, senior director of data center and AI networking at Meta. “Extending FBOSS to Spectrum ASICs means we can run that same software stack across our fabrics, and Meta’s new Spectrum-based switch, N-IceCube, brings that into Icepack – our liquid-cooled 102.4T network rack for scale-out that connects upcoming generations of accelerators in our fleet.” Together, Meta and NVIDIA are developing an architecture and operational playbook that other AI infrastructure operators can adopt, turning lessons from demanding production workloads into more scalable, resilient and efficient AI factories. With USFP, NVIDIA and Cisco Reinvent Pluggable Optics for AI Factory Scale As AI factories scale to support larger models and surging inference demand, every component of the infrastructure stack must deliver more performance, efficiency and simplicity — right down to the network connection itself. At OCP, NVIDIA and Cisco announced plans for USFP, a new optical pluggable transceiver module form factor designed to help AI factory builders scale next-generation AI fabrics while improving bandwidth density and power efficiency. With approximately the same footprint as the widely adopted 200Gb/s-per-lane OSFP form factor, USFP will provide a path to 400Gb/s-per-lane networking and will extend a transceiver-based deployment model already proven across generations of data center networks. Packing 16 full-duplex lanes with plans to scale up to 32 lanes, USFP will deliver four times the bandwidth density of traditional 200Gb/s-per-lane pluggable optics. The result is the ability to connect more compute resources without adding network tiers that can increase latency, power consumption and complexity. The new form factor is designed for the scale and efficiency demands of next generation AI factories, supporting higher-bandwidth fabrics while preserving the flexibility and serviceability that have made pluggable optics a mainstay of modern data centers. It also will deliver roughly 1.3x greater power efficiency, helping operators move more data with less energy. To help drive an open ecosystem, NVIDIA and Cisco are collaborating with TE Connectivity and Amphenol on cages, connectors and modules, with plans to advance USFP through a community-led, multi-source effort. Together, the companies are laying the foundation for more scalable, efficient and interoperable AI factory networking. Google Falcon Transport Supports NVIDIA ConnectX-10 for Interoperable AI Networking NVIDIA and Google also announced Falcon Transport support on future NVIDIA ConnectX-10 SuperNICs and BlueField DPUs, helping improve network efficiency for large-scale AI infrastructure. Falcon is a transport protocol designed to deliver data reliably over Ethernet networks, which can otherwise drop packets under congestion. It supports AI and storage workloads through multipath load balancing, programmable congestion control, hardware loss recovery and per-connection security. This collaboration combines NVIDIA hardware acceleration with DOCA software to implement Falcon and extend NVIDIA networking to Google’s data center transport. NVIDIA and Google NICs can communicate over a common transport while applications retain standard RDMA programming interfaces. By distributing traffic across paths, adapting to congestion, recovering dropped packets and protecting connections, Falcon helps workloads make better use of available bandwidth and maintain predictable performance as Ethernet fabrics scale. Learn more by joining NVIDIA at OCP .

title: Rally Up: ‘Gears of War: E-Day’ Launches on GeForce NOW
text: Gears of War: E-Day leads the charge on GeForce NOW this week, bringing Marcus Fenix and Dom Santiago’s first fight against the Locust Horde to the cloud with GeForce RTX-powered performance. title: Why Telecom Operators Are Building Their AI Strategy on Open Models
text: Telecom operators are increasingly building their AI strategies on open models — and the reasons go beyond mere cost. Open models give telcos the ability to trust, control and customize AI across their most critical workloads — from autonomous networks to customer care. NVIDIA’s latest State of AI in Telecommunications report reflects this shift, with 89% of respondents reporting that open source models and software are important to their company’s AI strategy. For operators, the strategic value of open models is fivefold: They expand access to frontier‑level intelligence at lower cost, allowing operators to reserve closed models for the workloads where they drive the most value. Independent benchmarks such as the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v4.3.2 show that leading open models are becoming more competitive across demanding reasoning, coding, scientific and agentic workloads. They support telco‑specific customization, with open weights and training recipes that operators can fine‑tune for their own operations using network, customer and industry data. They enable trustworthy AI by giving telcos greater visibility into and control over model artifacts and behavior, so models can be evaluated, adapted and governed in alignment with regulations and business policies. They enable flexible, secure deployment: teams can size and optimize open models to run across public clouds, private infrastructure and edge environments. They unlock the opportunity for telcos to deliver locally adapted AI services to enterprise and government customers by hosting and fine-tuning open models. Open Foundations, Tuned for Telecom Operations The NVIDIA Nemotron family of open models provides frontier -level reasoning performance optimized for agentic workflows, as well as speech capabilities for voice applications, with open weights, training data and recipes. SoftBank Corp. illustrates how an operator can use open models as a basis for developing and continuously advancing its telecom-specific AI capabilities. “Open models allow SoftBank Corp. to build on the rapid progress of global foundation models while applying the network knowledge and operational expertise we have accumulated over many years,” said Rajeev Koodli, principal fellow of SoftBank Corp. and senior vice president of SB Telecom America. “We are using open foundations extensively, including NVIDIA Nemotron models and others, in developing our SoftBank Large Telecom Model, continuously advancing it for telecom-specific use cases such as network operations, design and overall management.” In addition, NVIDIA is collaborating with partners to help turn open models into practical building blocks for telecom AI. NVIDIA announced the 30-billion-parameter Nemotron 3 Large Telco Model (LTM), fine-tuned by AdaptKey on open source telecom datasets to deliver accuracy gains for telecom-specific tasks. This gives operators an open baseline that can understand telecom industry terminology and reason effectively through telecom operations workflows such as network configuration and customer incident triage. To help operators customize the Nemotron 3 LTM and other open models with their own operational data, NVIDIA released the full recipe that walks through the end-to-end fine-tuning pipeline for adapting open models to operator-specific networks, customers and procedures using NVIDIA NeMo open libraries. Scale Open Models Into Production Workflows Open models are a critical building block, but it takes more than models to bring autonomous telecom operations safely into production. For AT&T, the value of model choice lies in making that flexibility operational in alignment with its business priorities. “At AT&T, we believe the future of AI is not about choosing a single model; it’s about intelligently matching every workload to the right combination of performance, cost and control,” said Andy Markus, chief data and AI officer of AT&T. “Open models are essential to that approach, and with NVIDIA, we can bring that model-choice strategy into production with the scale, reliability and governance our business requires.” Operators need pipelines that prepare and protect their data for model fine‑tuning by anonymizing sensitive records and generating privacy‑preserving synthetic datasets. They also need a platform that can turn open models into governed, autonomous agentic workflows. NVIDIA provides that end-to-end platform , powered by NVIDIA AI Enterprise software and NVIDIA Agent Toolkit , and spanning data pipelines, open models, agent orchestration, secure runtimes and simulation. Together with a strong partner ecosystem building at every layer of this platform, telecom operators have a clear path to translate the benefits of open models into production-ready AI workflows. Create a Platform for Local AI Innovation As telecom operators build AI infrastructure aligned with national AI strategies , open models are giving them a foundation to deliver AI services tailored to local languages, industries, regulations and data governance requirements. Operators across countries can fine-tune open models for local-language and industry-specific needs, as well as host open models on their trusted platforms that customers can consume directly or build on with their own data and applications. For Indosat Ooredoo Hutchison, one of Indonesia’s largest telecom operators, that means building AI that reflects the country’s own language and culture through its Sahabat-AI family of open source models. “For countries like Indonesia, the value of open models goes beyond access to powerful AI. It is about adapting that intelligence to our own language, culture, data and real-world needs,” said Chirag Sukhadia, chief data and AI officer of Indosat Ooredoo Hutchison. “Sahabat-AI puts this into practice, using open models as a foundation to build AI that understands Indonesia and can be developed for local applications. This allows us not only to adopt AI, but to build capabilities around it and enable more Indonesians to create with AI on their own terms.” Learn more about NVIDIA technologies for telecommunications .

title: From Scan to Treatment Plan, AI Helps Close Breast Cancer’s Deadliest Gaps
text: Breast cancer is the most commonly diagnosed cancer among American women — yet the gaps in care are wide. A majority of women over age 40 skip the recommended annual screening. Radiologists are reading more mammograms with fewer colleagues. And when a diagnosis arrives, the tests that inform treatment can take weeks to return results. Startups across the U.S. are building AI applications to support clinicians at each of these friction points, including imaging, risk assessment and treatment planning. About 40 million mammograms are performed in the U.S. each year, but a projected shortfall of tens of thousands of radiologists over the next decade is straining the system’s capacity to read them. At the other end of the care timeline, treatment decisions often hinge on genomic assays sent off to outside labs — assays that take weeks to process, at a moment when speed and certainty matter most. The companies below, all members of the NVIDIA Inception program for startups, are addressing both ends of that gap, and everything in between, accelerated by NVIDIA AI infrastructure. Automated Imaging Delivers AI-Powered Insights For women struggling to find time or a nearby location for breast cancer screening, access is a practical barrier that translates into missed diagnoses. NVIDIA Inception startup iSono Health was built around simplifying this imaging workflow. The company’s FDA-cleared ATUSA platform — a wearable, automated 3D quantitative ultrasound system — captures a standardized breast volume in approximately two minutes per breast, compared with up to 45 minutes for a conventional handheld ultrasound. The system’s AI, trained on thousands of full-breast scans comprising over 1.5 million ultrasound frames, automates image acquisition. It uses NVIDIA GPU acceleration and open source medical imaging technology to deliver a 3D scan that the company says is 28% more sensitive than a handheld 2D ultrasound. https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/ATUSA_software_show_10s.mp4 Handheld ultrasound depends on whoever holds the probe, so a woman’s scans typically can’t be compared from one year to the next. ATUSA captures the whole breast the same way every time, creating a repeatable view of breast tissue that could help clinicians analyze how a patient’s tissue changes across successive scans, while also reducing operator errors and variability. ATUSA is commercially available through partner clinics across California, Texas, Georgia, Tennessee and Washington D.C., with new sites coming online regularly. “Getting the scan closer to the patient is the first breakthrough,” said Neda Razavi, CEO of iSono Health. “Our vision is to make that scan increasingly informative: helping clinicians see what is there, understand what has changed and make more informed decisions.” iSono Health has developed AI capabilities for lesion detection, 3D segmentation and lesion classification. It next plans to extend its AI pipeline into multimodal diagnostic intelligence spanning 3D ultrasound, mammography, MRI and clinical information. The company has a multicenter clinical study with 3,200 patients underway to further validate the platform’s performance, with lead research sites at UC Davis and Vanderbilt University Medical Center. Finding Cancers, Cutting False Alarms Another NVIDIA Inception company, Whiterabbit.ai, develops AI technology for breast cancer screening. Its FDA-cleared WRDensity software automatically assesses breast density from mammograms and has been used in the care of hundreds of thousands of patients. The company has also developed WRRisk, a clinical decision support software for estimating patients’ long-term risk of developing breast cancer — and is researching a new generation of AI for mammography that could help radiologists detect more cancers while automating the screening of mammograms that are negative for breast cancer. The goal is to reduce the burden on a strained radiologist workforce, accelerate results and reduce avoidable callbacks for patients, and lower downstream healthcare costs. Whiterabbit.ai’s FDA-cleared WRDensity software automatically assesses breast density from mammograms. “Every day, breast radiologists face a needle-in-a-haystack problem, trying to find roughly one cancer in every 200 mammograms,” said Jason Su, cofounder and chief technology officer of Whiterabbit.ai. “We hope AI can be a powerful sidekick to radiologists, helping to clear away the hay so they can focus their expertise where it matters most.” Whiterabbit trains its AI models on a cluster of NVIDIA GPUs housed at Washington University in St. Louis, supplemented by additional GPU capacity in the cloud. Inference runs on NVIDIA GPUs deployed directly in the clinic. Predicting Which Treatments Will Work Once a patient is diagnosed with breast cancer, the next question is what to do about it — and the answer depends on predicting how the cancer will respond to treatment. Today, these predictions are limited in scope and accuracy, and often require a separate tissue biopsy with a two- to four-week wait. Ataraxis AI is building clinical intelligence that predicts patient outcomes and response to different therapies using digital data, including pathology slides that are already part of the standard patient workup. Ataraxis’ AI models interpret patterns in pathology slides, visualized here as color-coded clusters. The models learn to associate variations among these patterns with differences in recurrence risk and chemosensitivity. “The tools oncologists rely on today to guide therapy decisions were largely trained once, fifteen years ago, and never updated. Our models get stronger every time we acquire more clinical trial data,” said Joseph Cappadona, member of technical staff at Ataraxis AI. “But as we scale our models, the bigger shift is being able to answer more questions to help oncologists personalize therapy across all cancers.” Ataraxis’s AI models analyze digital pathology slides and standard clinical variables to predict treatment response and recurrence risk. One model predicts whether presurgical chemotherapy is likely to shrink a patient’s tumor to the point of response before the operating room. After surgery, another model estimates a patient’s five-year recurrence risk and the likely benefit of chemotherapy as a next step. Both models have been validated across more than 10 institutions and multiple clinical trials, and are in active clinical use. They run on NVIDIA GPUs on premises, in an offsite data center and in the cloud — using PyTorch accelerated by NVIDIA CUDA throughout. Providing Tumor Insights With 3D Visualization Another NVIDIA Inception company, SimBioSys , joined NVIDIA on a recent panel marking Breast Cancer Awareness Month. The company builds AI-powered precision medicine technology that creates accurate 3D models of breast tumors, veins and other soft tissue, delivering important insights to help guide surgeries and influence treatment plans. It has also built a tool to estimate the risk of breast cancer recurrence based on 3D volumetric data from a patient’s breast MRI, tumor pathology and clinical data. “We’re building a platform that now allows us to take multimodal data — imaging exams, pathology results, genomic testing when applicable and other biological inputs — and, using AI, bring that all together,” said Stacey Stevens, CEO of SimBioSys, at the event. “When we do that, it generates new insights beyond what we had from any individual piece.” Stacey Stevens, CEO of SimBioSys, and Chelsea Sumner, healthcare AI startups lead for North and Latin America at NVIDIA, spoke on an October 1 panel in Phoenix, Arizona, on AI’s role in advancing breast cancer care. SimBioSys uses NVIDIA MONAI for training and validation data, and NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries including cuBLAS and MONAI Deploy for its imaging technology, which runs on NVIDIA GPUs in the cloud. “NVIDIA technology gives us the computing power to take hundreds or thousands of images, apply our AI and analyze them quickly,” Stevens said. “That speed matters because patients and physicians need answers quickly. They can’t afford to wait days or weeks.” The company’s work was also highlighted in a recent “ Good Morning America ” segment. Learn more about the NVIDIA Inception program for startups. Certain technologies described in this article are investigational and have not been approved by the U.S. FDA for commercial use.

“Every day, breast radiologists face a needle-in-a-haystack problem, trying to find roughly one cancer in every 200 mammograms,” said Jason Su, cofounder and chief technology officer of Whiterabbit.ai. “We hope AI can be a powerful sidekick to radiologists, helping to clear away the hay so they can focus their expertise where it matters most.”

Whiterabbit trains its AI models on a cluster of NVIDIA GPUs housed at Washington University in St. Louis, supplemented by additional GPU capacity in the cloud. Inference runs on NVIDIA GPUs deployed directly in the clinic.

Predicting Which Treatments Will Work

Once a patient is diagnosed with breast cancer, the next question is what to do about it — and the answer depends on predicting how the cancer will respond to treatment. 

Today, these predictions are limited in scope and accuracy, and often require a separate tissue biopsy with a two- to four-week wait. Ataraxis AI is building clinical intelligence that predicts patient outcomes and response to different therapies using digital data, including pathology slides that are already part of the standard patient workup.

“The tools oncologists rely on today to guide therapy decisions were largely trained once, fifteen years ago, and never updated. Our models get stronger every time we acquire more clinical trial data,” said Joseph Cappadona, member of technical staff at Ataraxis AI. “But as we scale our models, the bigger shift is being able to answer more questions to help oncologists personalize therapy across all cancers.”

Ataraxis’s AI models analyze digital pathology slides and standard clinical variables to predict treatment response and recurrence risk. One model predicts whether presurgical chemotherapy is likely to shrink a patient’s tumor to the point of response before the operating room. After surgery, another model estimates a patient’s five-year recurrence risk and the likely benefit of chemotherapy as a next step. 

Both models have been validated across more than 10 institutions and multiple clinical trials, and are in active clinical use. They run on NVIDIA GPUs on premises, in an offsite data center and in the cloud — using PyTorch accelerated by NVIDIA CUDA throughout.

Providing Tumor Insights With 3D Visualization

Another NVIDIA Inception company, SimBioSys, joined NVIDIA on a recent panel marking Breast Cancer Awareness Month. 

The company builds AI-powered precision medicine technology that creates accurate 3D models of breast tumors, veins and other soft tissue, delivering important insights to help guide surgeries and influence treatment plans. It has also built a tool to estimate the risk of breast cancer recurrence based on 3D volumetric data from a patient’s breast MRI, tumor pathology and clinical data. 

“We’re building a platform that now allows us to take multimodal data — imaging exams, pathology results, genomic testing when applicable and other biological inputs — and, using AI, bring that all together,” said Stacey Stevens, CEO of SimBioSys, at the event. “When we do that, it generates new insights beyond what we had from any individual piece.”

SimBioSys uses NVIDIA MONAI for training and validation data, and NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries including cuBLAS and MONAI Deploy for its imaging technology, which runs on NVIDIA GPUs in the cloud. 

“NVIDIA technology gives us the computing power to take hundreds or thousands of images, apply our AI and analyze them quickly,” Stevens said. “That speed matters because patients and physicians need answers quickly. They can’t afford to wait days or weeks.”

The company’s work was also highlighted in a recent “Good Morning America” segment.

Learn more about the NVIDIA Inception program for startups.

Certain technologies described in this article are investigational and have not been approved by the U.S. FDA for commercial use.

title: NVIDIA DGX Spark 64GB Gives Developers More Ways to Build and Scale Local AI
text: Local AI is becoming more useful by the token. As AI agents move from experiments into everyday development, increasingly capable open models are shrinking to fit on more devices, giving builders more to run locally. Coming this month, NVIDIA DGX Spark will be available with 64GB of unified memory from top manufacturer partners — Acer, ASUS, Dell, Gigabyte, HP and MSI — giving developers, researchers and AI enthusiasts a new configuration with DGX OS and the NVIDIA AI software stack ready to use from day one. The new SKU runs capable local agents on device — privately, without cloud dependency. And when workloads grow, two units can cluster together via NVIDIA Sync Cluster Assistant without any additional setup. It’s a complete local AI platform for agents, inference, fine-tuning, data science and edge development. The compact, personal AI supercomputer provides a place to experiment with models and developers’ own data without turning to a cloud instance for every task. The new 64GB configuration, available exclusively from manufacturer partners, keeps the platform at an accessible price point while retaining the GB10 Grace Blackwell Superchip, DGX OS and full NVIDIA AI software stack — same as the 128GB model. It supports up to 100-billion-parameter models and the agentic applications built on them, fully on device. Two 64GB units clustered together don’t just double the memory. In NVIDIA’s Qwen 3.8 27B test, two clustered 64 GB systems delivered up to 1.7x performance compared with a single system, with room to keep scaling as workloads demand. DGX Spark ships ready for agent development from day one — NVIDIA Agent Toolkit, CUDA-X AI libraries, Nemotron open models, and popular runtimes like Ollama, vLLM, and PyTorch with CUDA are all supported out of the box. The same workflow that ran on one unit scales to two without reconfiguring the software environment. title: How NVIDIA GPUs Help Accelerate OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra Ultrafast
text: GPT-6 Astra Ultrafast, running on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs , is available now in the OpenAI API and to eligible ChatGPT Work and Codex users. Accelerated by inference optimizations through OpenAI’s models that tap into the capabilities of the NVIDIA Blackwell architecture, Ultrafast offers up to 8x faster token generation than the Astra Standard mode. For developers, faster generation can shorten coding agents’ edit-test-debug cycles, reduce the time spent generating responses between tool calls and make interactive applications feel more responsive. A faster response matters most when it’s repeated across a workflow: an agent writes code, uses a tool, checks the result and decides what to do next. Ultrafast brings Astra’s capabilities into these time-sensitive loops. NVIDIA AI infrastructure helps OpenAI serve more useful model outputs when developers need it. “NVIDIA’s deep investment in tooling and documentation has enabled us to make our models exceptionally good at programming Blackwell and Rubin GPUs,” said Philippe Tillet, inference lead at OpenAI. “Astra can turn that knowledge into high-performance kernels that make NVIDIA hardware compelling across the full frontier of latency, throughput and cost. With Astra Ultrafast, that means faster model responses as agents write code, use tools and work through complex tasks.” Continually Improving Performance Performance gains don’t stop when a model is deployed. OpenAI is using its own models to help refine the inference software running on NVIDIA GPUs, taking advantage of the platform’s programmability to test and implement improvements. That ongoing work can make model responses faster and deployed infrastructure more productive over time. “Our work with NVIDIA is helping us make AI faster and more useful,” said Uday Ruddarraju, chief technology officer of compute at OpenAI. “We used our internal models to optimize inference on NVIDIA GPUs, and NVIDIA’s programmability helped us deliver the acceleration behind Astra Ultrafast.” A programmable NVIDIA platform allows developers and researchers to reuse infrastructure across training, inference and reinforcement learning as models evolve. That flexibility helps teams repurpose compute resources as demand changes, improving utilization and avoiding overprovision for each workload. Developers can use GPT-6 Astra Ultrafast through the API today. See the Ultrafast guide for access, pricing and implementation details.

title: Productive, Durable, Fungible: How NVIDIA AI Factories Maximize Return on Investment
text: AI factories are built by the megawatt, even by the gigawatt. Each megawatt factory costs roughly $60 million, and AI factory operators will only commit capital on that scale with a clear view of the return on investment. Three key things shape AI factory returns: Earning capacity: What the factory could earn in a year if it sold every token it can produce. Useful life : How long its AI hardware keeps earning. Demand : How much demand there is for those tokens. Strength cannot fully offset weakness in another. High earning capacity counts for little if the factory sells only part of what it can produce. High demand matters little if it stops producing at full capacity in just a year. Nor are the three independent. A factory that can run more kinds of workloads finds more demand, keeping it earning year after year. NVIDIA AI factories are engineered to maximize all three. They’re: Productive : Delivering the highest throughput per megawatt and the lowest cost per token, which maximizes their earning capacity . Durable : NVIDIA GPUs and systems keep earning years after they ship, extending useful life . Fungible : They run every type of AI — in every phase and every place — as well as many workloads that don’t involve AI at all, which deepens and broadens the demand they can serve. NVIDIA platform is productive, durable and fungible, which maximizes AI factory returns. Engineering codesign across the full stack maximizes AI factory throughput, and continuous software optimization keeps installed hardware productive years after it ships. NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries let a factory run any accelerated workload. A standardized architecture then puts all of it within reach of any operator, deployable from a validated reference design. Productive: Highest Tokens Per Megawatt and Lowest Token Cost Power is the binding constraint on an AI factory. This makes tokens per second per megawatt the number that governs earning capacity. More tokens inside a fixed power envelope means more revenue. Lower cost per token means more margin on it. SemiAnalysis AgentX data shows NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 systems deliver over 30x higher throughput per megawatt than NVIDIA GB300 NVL72, and up to 45x lower cost per million tokens on the DeepSeek V4 Pro model. Gains of that size come from extreme codesign across the full stack: from models and workloads down through software to compute, networking and memory, all optimized together.   1. Earning capacity: What the factory could earn in a year if it sold every token it can produce.
  2. Useful life: How long its AI hardware keeps earning.
  3. Demand: How much demand there is for those tokens.

Strength cannot fully offset weakness in another. High earning capacity counts for little if the factory sells only part of what it can produce. High demand matters little if it stops producing at full capacity in just a year. Nor are the three independent. A factory that can run more kinds of workloads finds more demand, keeping it earning year after year.

NVIDIA AI factories are engineered to maximize all three. They’re:  

  • Productive: Delivering the highest throughput per megawatt and the lowest cost per token, which maximizes their earning capacity.

title: NVIDIA Opens Applications for 2027–2028 Graduate Fellowships With Awards Up to $60,000
text: Bringing together the world’s brightest minds and the latest accelerated computing technology leads to powerful breakthroughs that help tackle some of the biggest research problems. To foster such innovation, the NVIDIA Graduate Fellowship Program provides grants, mentors and technical support to doctoral students doing outstanding research relevant to NVIDIA technologies. The program, in its 26th year, is now accepting applications worldwide. It focuses on supporting students working in AI, machine learning, autonomous vehicles, computer graphics, robotics, healthcare, high-performance computing and related fields. Awards are up to $60,000 per student. Since its start in 2002, the Graduate Fellowship Program has awarded over 220 grants worth around $8 million. Students must have completed at least their first year of Ph.D.-level studies at the time of application. The application deadline for the 2027-2028 academic year is October 30, 2026. An in-person internship at an NVIDIA research office preceding the fellowship year is mandatory; eligible candidates must be available for the internship in summer 2027. For more on eligibility and how to apply, visit the program website . Featured image shows last year’s NVIDIA Graduate Fellowship recipients.

title: From Training to Production, NVIDIA and CoreWeave Close the Loop on Agentic AI
text: Building on nearly a decade of co-engineering, CoreWeave has built NVIDIA compute, networking and software into a cloud purpose-built for AI that’s still returning on investment across multiple generations of deployment. Now, CoreWeave is bringing the next generation of NVIDIA infrastructure to production. At CoreWeave Fully Connected, running this week in San Francisco, CoreWeave announced availability of NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 systems with Spectrum-X 102.4T Ethernet networking.
