title: Privacy's Defenders Podcast: No Privacy Without Encryption
text: When we communicate online today – from your personal emails and DMs to secure international commerce – we usually do so with encryption. Encryption converts readable data into unreadable gibberish to protect our privacy and security. This didn’t just happen organically. Three decades ago, the U.S government treated encryption like a weapon, and it took some unlikely heroes to set it free: a grad student, a junior lawyer, and a fledgling digital rights group who sued the federal government. The ruling in Bernstein v. Department of Justice held that code is speech and so is protected by the First Amendment – a precedent that underpins the internet as we know it today. This landmark case was led by Cindy Cohn, then a young pro bono lawyer working on behalf of EFF, who went on to become EFF’s legal director and then executive director. Welcome to the second episode of “Privacy’s Defenders,” a podcast about the people – lawyers, journalists, hackers, and others – who’ve fought to secure your digital liberties since before most people even knew what the internet was. Privacy info. This embed will serve content from simplecast.com (You can also find this episode on the Internet Archive and on YouTube .) In this episode, Cindy – who left EFF in June – speaks with Dan Bernstein, who was a Cal Berkeley grad student when he developed a simple encryption algorithm called “Snuffle.” Because federal law classified encryption as a war munition, publishing Snuffle meant submitting it to the government for review, getting a license as an arms dealer, and being granted a license the government had no intention of granting. Bernstein felt this violated his free-speech rights and in 1995 he sued, represented by Cindy working with EFF. Cindy also talks with Tony Coppolino, the Justice Department lawyer she battled in court – who admits she intimidated him from their very first phone call, and who offers a surprising perspective on the case all these years later. The “Privacy’s Defenders” podcast is a follow-up to Cindy’s book, “ Privacy’s Defender: My Thirty-Year Fight Against Digital Surveillance ,” bringing to life pivotal moments in the voices of those who fought for your rights. Sales of “Privacy’s Defender” benefit EFF, so pick up your copy today ! Joanne Elgart Jennings co-produced and created this podcast. Jarrod Sport co-produced, mixed, and mastered it. Corinne Ruff is our story editor. We had additional help from Rachel Estabrook and Alison Broverman. The original music was composed and performed by Nat Keefe of Hot Buttered Rum with Ben Andrews on the fiddle.

title: Resisting the Menace of Federal Data Consolidation
text: In the past two years, the federal government has unlawfully consolidated data exposing our private information. This consolidation has been chaotic but generally came in three rolling waves: It started with DOGE, moved to agency-to-agency data sharing with ICE, and then attempted data-driven purges of state voter rolls. We all deserve to live in a world where the data we use to pay our taxes, receive benefits, and vote is not combined and weaponized against us. The amalgamation of data leads to mistakes, abuses, and a lack of trust in institutions meant to protect us. Overall, it can chill our participation in society. This is particularly true for groups disfavored by this administration—especially immigrants and protesters. Congress highlighted similar abuses—including the creation of enemies lists and snooping on activists and federal employees—following the McCarthy and Watergate eras. And the increasing use of computers to magnify those harms led Congress to pass a slate of protections like the federal Privacy Act of 1974. The good news is that many people have stepped forward to resist the federal government’s unprecedented and unlawful data consolidations. Many groups, including EFF, have filed lawsuits to enforce our data privacy laws, and many states have, too. Legislators at the federal and state levels have worked to expose and oppose these surveillance programs. And many people have protested for their right to data privacy. Existing data privacy protections have been essential in the past two years, but they can be improved . This should include: narrowing loopholes and increasing enforcement in existing laws, limiting the government’s purchase of data on the commercial market, and passing a comprehensive consumer privacy law. Data Consolidation by DOGE Starting on January 20, 2025, President Trump created DOGE —essentially renaming an existing agency originally meant to modernize government technology. Rather than engage in modernization, DOGE quickly obtained high-level access to sensitive databases across the government that store millions of people’s personal records—including at the Office of Personnel Management (OPM), the Social Security Administration , and the Treasury Department . DOGE was staffed with people with little government or cybersecurity knowledge and who often had conflicts of interest. DOGE’s early aim was not always clear, aside from gaining “ prompt access to all unclassified agency records ” and the “ sharing and consolidation ” of those records. The result? The indiscriminate firing of government employees and the decimation of important agencies that focused on consumer protection and foreign aid . It also resulted in clear misuses of data. For example, while working with DOGE at the Social Security Administration, one individual signed an outside agreement with an advocacy group with the aim of using SSA data to find evidence of alleged voter fraud and “ overturn election results in certain States .” DOGE’s data access and consolidation violated the federal Privacy Act , which limits the sharing and consolidation of government databases. Many groups stepped in to sue . For example, EFF and our co-counsel at Lex Lumina LLC and Democracy Defenders Fund , on behalf of two public employee unions ( AFGE and AALJ ), sued the OPM for unlawfully disclosing federal workers’ information to DOGE. After EFF and others secured early victories , the government sought to end the lawsuits by firing many DOGE agents and removing their access to records. A great deal of damage remains in need of a judicial remedy. Data Consolidation by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Even as DOGE’s influence diminished, federal agencies have attempted to share, compare, and seize large databases, in order to target immigrants. In some cases, they have succeeded. This happened with tax records at the IRS , Medicaid data from the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), and public housing data from the Department of Housing and Urban Development . The Department of Agriculture also sought to collect databases regarding Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Programs (SNAP) from states. Many groups have filed lawsuits to block this anti-immigrant-motivated data consolidation, alleging it violates privacy protection laws. EFF filed amicus briefs in support of two of these lawsuits: Centro de Trabajadores v. Bessent , which concerns IRS data; and California v. HHS , which concerns Medicaid data (and where we teamed up with EPIC and Protect Democracy ). Most recently, states have stepped up to challenge the federal government’s attempted seizure, for immigration enforcement purposes, of state commercial driver’s license data held by the American Association of Motor Vehicle Administrators, a non-profit organization. This data consolidation for immigration enforcement has also included government purchase of commercial products. This includes ICE’s purchase of commercial location data without a warrant, and its interest in “ Big Data and Ad Tech providers .” ICE also has contracts with companies like Palantir , which help organize all the datasets the agency collects. Data Consolidation for Voter Purges The right to vote is fundamental to every democracy. That’s why EFF has long advocated for cybersecurity in voting systems , to make sure every vote is properly counted. Voter purges are a longstanding threat to the right to vote. State and local officials regularly delete people from the voter registration rolls, often for bad reasons and without adequate notice. This has a disparate impact against people of color. Now the federal government is trying to purge voters, too. To do so, it has consolidated our data in three ways. First, it is using an old data system called SAVE for a new purpose: checking voter eligibility. Second, it has seized voter information from states. Third, it has created a federal list of eligible voters. As a direct result, people with a right to vote will be purged from voter rolls because of erroneous data. Others will be intimidated from voting or registering. And all registered voters suffer a violation of their data privacy rights: information collected for one purpose is being used against them for another purpose. Expansion of SAVE Since 1986, the federal government has operated SAVE , which stands for Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements. It is not a database, but it facilitates easy access to databases. It is used to determine whether immigrants and naturalized citizens are eligible for various government benefits, such as food stamps. In 2025, the federal government started using SAVE for a new purpose : checking voters’ eligibility. Further, SAVE now provides access to new databases and allows bulk searches. More than 60 million voters have been run through SAVE, and 21,000 were flagged as potential noncitizens who are ineligible to vote. Erroneous flags have caused purges of lawful voters – such as Anthony Nell . A case called League of Women Voters v. DHS challenges this expansion of SAVE. The plaintiffs are represented by CREW , Democracy Forward , the Fair Elections Center , and EPIC. A federal judge held this program unlawful and set it aside. DHS appealed and asked for a stay of this order, and a federal appellate court denied the stay. Unfortunately, the U.S. Supreme Court granted the stay, exercising its controversial “ shadow docket ” authority by a six-to-three vote. Federal employees in DHS’s “ Fraud Detection and National Security Unit ,” which ordinarily investigates alleged immigration fraud, have been re-assigned to examine voter eligibility . A whistleblower alleges that employees have been directed to go to state election agency websites, enter some of a voter’s personal information, and thereby access more of it. In the past two years, the federal government has unlawfully consolidated data exposing our private information. 

This consolidation has been chaotic but generally came in three rolling waves: It started with DOGE, moved to agency-to-agency data sharing with ICE, and then attempted data-driven purges of state voter rolls.

We all deserve to live in a world where the data we use to pay our taxes, receive benefits, and vote is not combined and weaponized against us. The amalgamation of data leads to mistakes, abuses, and a lack of trust in institutions meant to protect us. Overall, it can chill our participation in society. This is particularly true for groups disfavored by this administration—especially immigrants and protesters.

Congress highlighted similar abuses—including the creation of enemies lists and snooping on activists and federal employees—following the McCarthy and Watergate eras. And the increasing use of computers to magnify those harms led Congress to pass a slate of protections like the federal Privacy Act of 1974.

The good news is that many people have stepped forward to resist the federal government’s unprecedented and unlawful data consolidations. Many groups, including EFF, have filed lawsuits to enforce our data privacy laws, and many states have, too. Legislators at the federal and state levels have worked to expose and oppose these surveillance programs. And many people have protested for their right to data privacy.

Existing data privacy protections have been essential in the past two years, but they can be improved. This should include: narrowing loopholes and increasing enforcement in existing laws, limiting the government’s purchase of data on the commercial market, and passing a comprehensive consumer privacy law.

Data Consolidation by DOGE

Starting on January 20, 2025, President Trump created DOGE—essentially renaming an existing agency originally meant to modernize government technology. Rather than engage in modernization, DOGE quickly obtained high-level access to sensitive databases across the government that store millions of people’s personal records—including at the Office of Personnel Management (OPM), the Social Security Administration, and the Treasury Department.

DOGE was staffed with people with little government or cybersecurity knowledge and who often had conflicts of interest. DOGE’s early aim was not always clear, aside from gaining “prompt access to all unclassified agency records” and the “sharing and consolidation” of those records.

The result? The indiscriminate firing of government employees and the decimation of important agencies that focused on consumer protection and foreign aid. It also resulted in clear misuses of data. For example, while working with DOGE at the Social Security Administration, one individual signed an outside agreement with an advocacy group with the aim of using SSA data to find evidence of alleged voter fraud and “overturn election results in certain States.”

DOGE’s data access and consolidation violated the federal Privacy Act, which limits the sharing and consolidation of government databases. Many groups stepped in to sue. For example, EFF and our co-counsel at Lex Lumina LLC and Democracy Defenders Fund, on behalf of two public employee unions (AFGE and AALJ), sued the OPM for unlawfully disclosing federal workers’ information to DOGE. After EFF and others secured early victories, the government sought to end the lawsuits by firing many DOGE agents and removing their access to records. A great deal of damage remains in need of a judicial remedy.

Data Consolidation by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS)

Even as DOGE’s influence diminished, federal agencies have attempted to share, compare, and seize large databases, in order to target immigrants. In some cases, they have succeeded. This happened with tax records at the IRS, Medicaid data from the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), and public housing data from the Department of Housing and Urban Development. The Department of Agriculture also sought to collect databases regarding Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Programs (SNAP) from states.

Many groups have filed lawsuits to block this anti-immigrant-motivated data consolidation, alleging it violates privacy protection laws. EFF filed amicus briefs in support of two of these lawsuits: Centro de Trabajadores v. Bessent, which concerns IRS data; and California v. HHS, which concerns Medicaid data (and where we teamed up with EPIC and Protect Democracy). Most recently, states have stepped up to challenge the federal government’s attempted seizure, for immigration enforcement purposes, of state commercial driver’s license data held by the American Association of Motor Vehicle Administrators, a non-profit organization.

This data consolidation for immigration enforcement has also included government purchase of commercial products. This includes ICE’s purchase of commercial location data without a warrant, and its interest in “Big Data and Ad Tech providers.” ICE also has contracts with companies like Palantir, which help organize all the datasets the agency collects.

Data Consolidation for Voter Purges

The right to vote is fundamental to every democracy. That’s why EFF has long advocated for cybersecurity in voting systems, to make sure every vote is properly counted.

Voter purges are a longstanding threat to the right to vote. State and local officials regularly delete people from the voter registration rolls, often for bad reasons and without adequate notice. This has a disparate impact against people of color.

Now the federal government is trying to purge voters, too. To do so, it has consolidated our data in three ways. First, it is using an old data system called SAVE for a new purpose: checking voter eligibility. Second, it has seized voter information from states. Third, it has created a federal list of eligible voters.

As a direct result, people with a right to vote will be purged from voter rolls because of erroneous data. Others will be intimidated from voting or registering. And all registered voters suffer a violation of their data privacy rights: information collected for one purpose is being used against them for another purpose.

Expansion of SAVE

Since 1986, the federal government has operated SAVE, which stands for Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements. It is not a database, but it facilitates easy access to databases. It is used to determine whether immigrants and naturalized citizens are eligible for various government benefits, such as food stamps.

In 2025, the federal government started using SAVE for a new purpose: checking voters’ eligibility. Further, SAVE now provides access to new databases and allows bulk searches. More than 60 million voters have been run through SAVE, and 21,000 were flagged as potential noncitizens who are ineligible to vote. Erroneous flags have caused purges of lawful voters – such as Anthony Nell.

A case called League of Women Voters v. DHS challenges this expansion of SAVE. The plaintiffs are represented by CREW, Democracy Forward, the Fair Elections Center, and EPIC. A federal judge held this program unlawful and set it aside. DHS appealed and asked for a stay of this order, and a federal appellate court denied the stay. Unfortunately, the U.S. Supreme Court granted the stay, exercising its controversial “shadow docket” authority by a six-to-three vote.

Federal employees in DHS’s “Fraud Detection and National Security Unit,” which ordinarily investigates alleged immigration fraud, have been re-assigned to examine voter eligibility. A whistleblower alleges that employees have been directed to go to state election agency websites, enter some of a voter’s personal information, and thereby access more of it. This may violate state laws requiring a person, before accessing a voter’s information, to attest they are that voter or have that voter’s authorization.

Since 2025, the federal government has demanded that at least 48 states hand over their voter information. At least 16 states have complied. The federal government is running this information through SAVE, searching for voters to purge.

The federal government has sued 30 states for refusing to comply. So far, courts have dismissed 25 of these suits. There’s also a lawsuit against this data grab, titled Common Cause v. DOJ, brought by CREW, Protect Democracy, and the ACLU.

The New Federal Voter Eligibility List

In March 2026, President Trump issued an executive order requiring DHS to create a list of people who are U.S. citizens, aged 18 or older, and residents of the state. The order also requires DOJ to prosecute anyone, including state and local officials, who provides a ballot to a person who is not eligible to vote in federal elections.

In California v. Trump, 24 states allege that this executive order violates the Constitution’s separation of powers. A federal judge enjoined this program, and an appellate court denied a stay. But the U.S. Supreme Court by a six-to-three vote granted a stay, which allows the program to move forward. (By a seven-to-two vote, the Court denied a stay of an injunction against a different part of the same executive order, which concerned mail-in ballots.) Another legal challenge, titled EPIC v. USCIS, alleges that the new federal voter eligibility list violates the Privacy Act as well as the separation of powers.

Next Steps

It is encouraging to see so many people, groups, and states step forward to protect our data privacy from these unlawful waves of federal data consolidations. Still, more work remains. For example:

  • The Privacy Act of 1974 has proven a critical bulwark. But after a half century, it could use a refresh. For example, Congress should close its loopholes and expand its enforceability.
  • Law enforcement agencies must be prohibited from avoiding the Constitution’s warrant requirement by buying our personal data from brokers. For example, Congress should pass the “Fourth Amendment Is Not For Sale Act.”
  • We need a comprehensive consumer data privacy law, among other reasons to reduce the flood of our personal data that corporations provide to law enforcement agencies. Legislators should check out EFF’s “privacy first” framework.

In the meantime, there’s no time like the present to practice surveillance self-defense, like using strong passwords and disabling your phone’s ad identification.

title: Organizing in the Town at Oakland Tech Week
text: EFF was thrilled to join organizers, advocates, and activists in the East Bay for the second annual Oakland Tech Week last week. We are grateful to our friends at MediaJustice and Upturn for inviting us co-present this all-day event, “Building Beyond Big Tech: Organizing Oakland’s Future” , on Sept. 30. The event, hosted by the Kapor Center in downtown Oakland, offered a unique chance to spend time with people across The Town and the Bay Area working to create a better future for everyone. “We’re at this truly consequential moment,” said EFF executive director Nicole Ozer, in her speech kicking off the day’s events. “We know that in this community’s work—and communities across the country—our ability to ensure that technology empowers rather than oppresses is fundamental to the future of countries, our livelihoods, and, literally, our lives.” We also participated in a panel on the state of play in California, moderated by MediaJustice executive director Steven Renderos. Director of State Affairs Hayley Tsukayama joined reporter Khari Johnson of CalMatters and Crystal Zemero of People Over Billionaires to talk about the landscape at the state level. The day also included smaller conversations focused on building better tech and fine-tuning messaging, facilitated by our colleagues at MediaJustice. Seeing the people—our neighbors—who are fighting back against surveillance in their communities was inspiring. They’re casting doubt on the claims large technology companies make about what’s happening in their neighborhoods. They’re speaking up at council meetings and rallies. They’re seeking changes that would give their workplaces and neighborhoods a better, safer relationship with technology. It was so important to come together in solidarity to compare notes, spend time together, find opportunities to support each other, and scheme together. We can work together to build a future that works for everyday people . A better world is possible—and Oakland Tech Week was a great reminder that, all around us, folks are working together to tackle huge challenges. “There are formidable forces,” Ozer said. “But we can pierce the other side’s narrative of inevitability with our power of indignation. The future of AI and other technology is not written and we can work together to get it right.” Whether you’re in Oakland or Aukland, consider this a renewed invitation to join us . Join the Fight Become an EFF Member Today

title: Turkish Crackdown On LGBTQ+ Organizations Threatens Freedom of Expression and Association
text: EFF strongly condemns Turkey’s state-led discriminatory, oppressive attacks on feminist and LGBTQ+ organisations, media platforms, student groups, and rights defenders and activists within the country. Since mid-September, access to the websites and social media accounts of a dozen organizations have been blocked by court order , while over 60 members and activists have been detained, their offices and homes raided , mobile phones, laptops and other digital devices seized, and judicial proceedings launched against them. These actions threaten the very existence of the LGBTQ+ organizations targeted, limiting their ability to carry out legitimate human rights work, deterring participation and support, and chilling the free speech rights of not just these groups, but any organization that even reports on LGBTQ+ oppression. A little over a week ago, an Istanbul court shut down the website and social media accounts of T24 , Turkey’s longest running independent digital news organization—which has covered government-backed campaigns against and earlier crackdowns on gay rights groups—alleging it had aired “LGBT propaganda” over the past year. It’s all part of Turkey’s efforts to portray LGBTQ+ groups and support networks for those living with HIV as criminal organizations that must be suppressed, purportedly to protect family values. Homosexuality is not illegal in Turkey (unlike Uganda , Nigeria , and Egypt , where it is criminalized), but LGBTQ+ organizations and activists have in recent years faced increased government oppression , including criminal proceedings on allegations related to obscenity and violations of Turkey’s Law on Associations, which regulates the activities of nonprofits. In its new crackdown, the government is targeting LGBTQ+ groups’ websites and social media channels for alleged obscene posts accessible to children. Kaos GL, Turkey’s oldest gay rights organization, said investigations are being led by the Cyber Crimes Bureau of the Ankara Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office , which took members of its Board of Directors into custody, raided their homes, and searched the organization’s offices, where electronic devices were seized. According to Human Rights Watch , prosecutors in Istanbul said those targeted were suspected of “founding, leading, or being a member of a criminal organization,” as well as sex work and drug-related offenses. Publicly available law enforcement and judicial documents about the investigation reportedly don’t say which publications or posts are alleged to be obscene. The prosecutor’s office launched an investigation of the organization and others under Article 226 of the Turkish Penal Code , which regulates the offense of “obscenity” (without clearly defining it), while the overall operation, dubbed “My Family is Safe” and launched as part of President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan’s “Decade of the Family” program, is being brought under Article 220 of the code. Justifying the crackdown by invoking family values and child safety suggests that the government is trying to enforce a moral code on society based on intolerance of and discrimination against LGBTQ+ people. New Low for Turkey Framing the activities of LGBTQ+ rights organizations as violations of organized crime provisions is a new low for Turkey, where free speech and press freedoms have long been under attack. The implication from these raids and investigations is that the organizations’ legitimate civil society work advocating for the rights of queer people—monitoring human rights violations, offering legal aid, running news portals, sponsoring cultural events such as symposiums and film screenings, publishing an online magazine and supporting LGBTQ+ refugees—is suspected of being criminal threatens the basic human rights of the LGBTQ+ community in Turkey. These actions send a dangerous message to people and organizations exercising freedom of speech and association in support of queer people. Under the penal code, directing a criminal organization is punishable by five to ten years in prison, while merely being a member carries a sentence of two to five years. EFF joins hundreds of human, civil, LGBTQ+, and digital rights organizations around the world in calling for the immediate release of all those detained for exercising their rights to freedom of expression, association and legitimate human rights work, and the unblocking of all websites and social media accounts of affected organizations. For many LGBTQ+ individuals the world over, the internet can be a safer space for exploring identity, finding community, and seeking support. The anti-LGBTQ+ crackdown in Turkey is not happening in a vacuum—unfortunately we are seeing anti-LGBTQ+ bills restricting free expression and privacy, content moderation decisions that disproportionately impact LGBTQ+ users, and other forms of intolerance around the world. We urge international civil society and diplomatic partners to raise awareness of and to speak out against the crackdown, and to publicly show support for the legitimacy of Turkey’s LGBTQ+ organizations and the important work they do to ensure that queer people are safe and free.

title: When No ID Means No Internet: Age Verification and the Right to Access Information
text: This post was co-authored by Sheila B. Lalwani , a doctorate student and recent COMPASS Fellow hosted by EFF. Age verification proposals are often presented as a simple tradeoff: sacrifice a little privacy to better safeguard children online. But that framing overlooks a more fundamental question. What happens to people who cannot verify their age at all? This is particularly a problem when users are required to prove their age with identity documents. Age-related restrictions are developing quickly around the world. While they differ radically across jurisdictions, in the past year, we’ve witnessed a sharp uptick toward mandatory age assurance for social media access but also for other high-risk digital services. For example: In late 2025, Australia became the first country to implement a minimum age requirement for prohibiting children under age 16 from creating or holding social media accounts. India passed the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act that includes mandatory verifiable parental consent and has undertaken ongoing discussions for social media restriction. The United Kingdom passed the Online Safety Act requiring age verification across a swath of services hosting content considered harmful to users under 18. More than half the states across the U.S. have enacted age verification laws . An EU Commission ’s expert report recommends a ban on social media access for users under 13. It also recommends mandatory age verification for platforms to ensure that users are ‘age appropriate.’ The Access Problem Age verification laws that are predicated on the necessity of users possessing a current passport, driver’s license, credit card, or similar documents proving their identity exclude critical sections of populations. And this problem is global in nature: Millions of people lack government-issued identification or encounter regular challenges to obtaining or updating it. Roughly 15 million adult U.S. citizens lack a driver’s license, and a further 2.6 million lack any government photo ID ; leaving large groups blocked from online content or services. The UK has a similar predicament: proof-of-age checks are often reliant on passports, driver’s licenses, or other recognized alternatives, which can pose unique challenges to people without these documents. Much of the advocacy around age verification discusses the privacy harms of age verification. Yet these measures also threaten something more fundamental: equal access to information and the ability to exercise the right to freedom of expression. Unfortunately, age verification systems foster unequal access to information and provide an asymmetric solution to find essential information, build community, and weigh in on public discourse. As governments and companies increasingly require users to prove their age before accessing online services, these individuals risk being excluded from large parts of the internet altogether. Effects on Global Majority Countries Age verification laws reshape who can speak, who can access information, and who gets excluded from the digital public sphere. In other words, age verification is not a neutral safety measure: it presents a structural barrier to disproportionately exclude certain groups—particularly those in the global majority—and alters the architecture of global online expression. Some of these groups are already marginalized offline, and age verification extends that exclusion into digital spaces. For instance, 850 million people globally do not have ID . Most of these individuals exist in primarily low and middle income countries in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia. The World Bank points out that many are members of marginalized groups and more than half of those lacking access to identity documentation also have children whose births have not been registered. Women are particularly vulnerable and are 8% less likely than men to have an ID. Other vulnerable groups, such as adults in low income countries, are less likely to have an ID when they fall below 25 years, as are those with a primary school education or less or those in rural areas. A policy paper from EDRi points out that age verification laws provide quick tech solutions but overlook longstanding structural challenges and undermine the universality of the internet. The analysis finds that age verification laws have serious human rights implications and ironically harm the very individuals they deem to protect. Moreover, these laws depend on the collection of harmful mass data that human rights organizations, including EFF, is fighting against —and has for decades . For example: In Morocco , a push to restrict children’s access would ban under-13s from creating accounts on gaming platforms. This could potentially create challenges for those with IDs that have incomplete information concerning the year of birth. In addition, this push would also impact those who attempt to leave Morocco. In Egypt , the lack of ID cards has created challenges for minority groups such as the Baha’i. Stateless individuals would also struggle under age verification laws. The Rohingya , the world’s largest population of stateless people , often lack IDs . Kuwait’s Bidoon population also lacks proper identification materials. According to Amnesty International , this leads many to rely on standard civil identity cards, which can be restrictive. Nigeria launched a national program to provide ID cards to its population in 2007. Since then, 64.4 million have registered, but that represents just over 30% of the national population. The Kafala system, a practice in several countries across the Middle East , also introduces challenges for age verification laws. Under this legal framework, migrant workers’ legal residency and employment status are bound to a specific employer. This potentially leaves stateless persons or migrant workers vulnerable to forced labor and restricted movements. No ID, No Access Age verification laws are less about confirming the age of a user and more about creating barriers to online participation that many people cannot reliably scale. The net result is reduced access, more data collection, and an increased chance of unequal or mistaken exclusion from accessing information online. Nobody doubts the importance of protecting children online. While proponents assert that age verification laws protect minors from harmful material, online harassment, and digital addiction, these laws are not the solution. They subvert fundamental freedom of expression rights and pose significant privacy risks. EFF has long warned against age-gating the internet. Age verification technology itself is often inaccurate and privacy-invasive , and as more countries considering implementing ID-based checks , the risks move beyond censorship and surveillance toward excluding some people entirely. That’s why we’re working with groups in the U.S. and around the world to push back against these laws, and why we hope you join our effort. For more information on how to fight back against dangerous age verification laws, visit our resource hub at eff.org/age

In other words, age verification is not a neutral safety measure: it presents a structural barrier to disproportionately exclude certain groups—particularly those in the global majority—and alters the architecture of global online expression. Some of these groups are already marginalized offline, and age verification extends that exclusion into digital spaces.

For instance, 850 million people globally do not have ID. Most of these individuals exist in primarily low and middle income countries in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia. The World Bank points out that many are members of marginalized groups and more than half of those lacking access to identity documentation also have children whose births have not been registered. Women are particularly vulnerable and are 8% less likely than men to have an ID. Other vulnerable groups, such as adults in low income countries, are less likely to have an ID when they fall below 25 years, as are those with a primary school education or less or those in rural areas. 

A policy paper from EDRi points out that age verification laws provide quick tech solutions but overlook longstanding structural challenges and undermine the universality of the internet. The analysis finds that age verification laws have serious human rights implications and ironically harm the very individuals they deem to protect. Moreover, these laws depend on the collection of harmful mass data that human rights organizations, including EFF, is fighting against—and has for decades. 

For example:

  • In Morocco, a push to restrict children’s access would ban under-13s from creating accounts on gaming platforms. This could potentially create challenges for those with IDs that have incomplete information concerning the year of birth. In addition, this push would also impact those who attempt to leave Morocco.
  • In Egypt, the lack of ID cards has created challenges for minority groups such as the Baha’i.
  • Stateless individuals would also struggle under age verification laws. The Rohingya, the world’s largest population of stateless people, often lack IDs. 
  • Kuwait’s Bidoon population also lacks proper identification materials. According to Amnesty International, this leads many to rely on standard civil identity cards, which can be restrictive.  
  • Nigeria launched a national program to provide ID cards to its population in 2007. Since then, 64.4 million have registered, but that represents just over 30% of the national population.
  • The Kafala system, a practice in several countries across the Middle East, also introduces challenges for age verification laws. Under this legal framework, migrant workers’ legal residency and employment status are bound to a specific employer. This potentially leaves stateless persons or migrant workers vulnerable to forced labor and restricted movements. 

No ID, No Access

Age verification laws are less about confirming the age of a user and more about creating barriers to online participation that many people cannot reliably scale. The net result is reduced access, more data collection, and an increased chance of unequal or mistaken exclusion from accessing information online. 

Nobody doubts the importance of protecting children online. While proponents assert that age verification laws protect minors from harmful material, online harassment, and digital addiction, these laws are not the solution. They subvert fundamental freedom of expression rights and pose significant privacy risks.  

EFF has long warned against age-gating the internet. Age verification technology itself is often inaccurate and privacy-invasive, and as more countries considering implementing ID-based checks, the risks move beyond censorship and surveillance toward excluding some people entirely. That’s why we’re working with groups in the U.S. and around the world to push back against these laws, and why we hope you join our effort.

For more information on how to fight back against dangerous age verification laws, visit our resource hub at eff.org/age

title: An open letter to every family’s designated IT support
text: Almost every family has one. They’re the only ones who know which remote turns on the TV and which controls the volume and channels. They know what an HDMI cable actually does and where to plug it in. They’ve even fixed multiple phone issues within seconds through a little-known, well-kept secret procedure (turning it off and back on). Perhaps they are a parent, tech-savvy sibling, cool aunt or uncle, or close family friend. Whatever the relation, the role stays the same. They are the unpaid, on-call tech specialist for every relative’s forgotten password, printer jam, and device settings update. If this sounds like you, we would first like to thank you for doing a job you never signed up for. Second, we would like to share a simple way you can help your family and friends protect their privacy and security without adding more to your plate. A small settings change that makes a big differenc e With Android and iPhone’s latest releases, and Black Friday deals rapidly approaching, many people are upgrading their current phone to a newer model. As the family’s go-to tech helper, you’ll likely be setting up a few new devices in the near future. You already know the routine: connect to Wi-Fi, choose a language, and transfer data from the old phone to the new one. But beyond the steps you are prompted to take when setting up a new phone lies a quiet decision many people never think twice about: their default browser. While people in some regions, like Europe and Japan, get to choose their default browser when setting up a new phone, this is not the case everywhere . Most phones ship with a browser preinstalled and set as the default, ready to start collecting data and monetizing off user activity the minute it’s opened. Unless deliberately changed, that’s the browser that will be used moving forward. Not because it’s the best option, but because it’s already there. But remember, everyone can choose the browser they use, and as the designated tech whiz of the family, you can help inspire others to choose the right one. Choosing Firefox means choosing privacy from the very first tap. The browser is where the data lives A browser is the door to everything you do online, and depending on how it’s designed, it can see a lot. Every site visited. Every phrase searched. Every link tapped. As we socialize, work, and explore on our phones, the browser can be the biggest funnel of personal data leaving that device, and how it’s built determines who collects that data, who can sell it, and how long it sticks around. Privacy is the starting point for our browser, not an afterthought. Firefox is built on the principle that not even Mozilla should know which websites you visit or what you do there. Why Firefox is the right call Firefox is backed by Mozilla , a nonprofit-backed company with no shareholders to report to. Instead of chasing financial returns for a small group, Mozilla aims to provide an internet that truly puts people first. This means we limit the data we know about you and give you more choice about what data you share and when. This commitment to user privacy is built into the browser itself. On both Android and iOS , Enhanced Tracking Protection (ETP) is enabled by default, blocking known trackers every time you browse. This helps prevent advertisers and data brokers from following people across sites, no setup required. You can also adjust ETP to fit different needs, including turning it off altogether or activating Strict mode for even stronger protection. Control and choice are built in, too. Firefox has an easily accessible AI controls section where people can customize how AI features show up in the browser, or turn them off entirely – because AI should always be a choice , not a requirement. To carry these principles and protections across every link opened on a new phone, set Firefox as the default mobile browser in just a few taps. How to set Firefox as the default browser on Android and iOS Downloading the Firefox mobile app isn’t enough on its own, since most phones will keep opening links in whatever browser came preinstalled unless told otherwise. Here’s how to make Firefox the browser that actually opens by default. Make sure Firefox is installed on the device you’re working with before you begin. On Android : Open Firefox Tap the three-dot menu button. Tap Settings. In the General section, locate the Set default browser option. Tap the toggle next to Set as default browser to turn it on. Select Firefox from the listed options. Tap Set as default. On iOS : Open phone Settings. Tap Apps. Tap Default Apps. Tap Browser App. Select Firefox from the listed options. Once Firefox has been selected as the default browser, links tapped from messages, email, social media, or anywhere else will open in Firefox automatically. No additional steps required by your less tech-savvy family members and friends, and no relying on them to open the “right” browser every time they want to access the internet. A little help on day one, lasting benefits later The way a device is initially set up tends to stick. Whichever browser is already selected as default and whatever privacy settings are (or aren’t) adjusted on day one often just…stay that way. That’s a lot of reliance on whatever defaults the phone is purchased with. So this fall, whether you are setting up a shiny new Google Pixel 11 for your aunt, an iPhone 18 Pro for your brother, or any other model for any one of your non-paying tech support “clients,” take an extra five minutes to help them download Firefox and set it as their default browser. They can start their new device journey browsing with privacy, choice, and control built in. And you can check one more thing off your unofficial family IT to-do list. If this sounds like you, we would first like to thank you for doing a job you never signed up for. Second, we would like to share a simple way you can help your family and friends protect their privacy and security without adding more to your plate.

With Android and iPhone’s latest releases, and Black Friday deals rapidly approaching, many people are upgrading their current phone to a newer model. Choosing Firefox means choosing privacy from the very first tap.

A browser is the door to everything you do online, and depending on how it’s designed, it can see a lot. Every site visited. Every phrase searched. Every link tapped. As we socialize, work, and explore on our phones, the browser can be the biggest funnel of personal data leaving that device, and how it’s built determines who collects that data, who can sell it, and how long it sticks around.

Privacy is the starting point for our browser, not an afterthought. Firefox is built on the principle that not even Mozilla should know which websites you visit or what you do there.

Firefox is backed by Mozilla, a nonprofit-backed company with no shareholders to report to. Instead of chasing financial returns for a small group, Mozilla aims to provide an internet that truly puts people first.   • Tap Default Apps.
  • Tap Browser App. 
  • Select Firefox from the listed options.

So this fall, whether you are setting up a shiny new Google Pixel 11 for your aunt, an iPhone 18 Pro for your brother, or any other model for any one of your non-paying tech support “clients,” take an extra five minutes to help them download Firefox and set it as their default browser. They can start their new device journey browsing with privacy, choice, and control built in. And you can check one more thing off your unofficial family IT to-do list.

title: Firefox’s free built-in VPN uncaps data limit through January 2027
text: Whether you’re heading home to see family this winter or taking a well-earned break before the year wraps up, we want you to browse with a little more peace of mind. That’s why, as our gift to you, everyone using Firefox’s free built-in VPN gets unlimited data starting today, November 10, through January 31, 2027. Sign in with a Mozilla account and unlock extra privacy for all that shopping, travel planning, and everyday browsing, no gift receipt required. Using Firefox’s free built-in VPN makes it harder for websites to use your IP address to determine where you are, or connect your visits across the web. Most importantly, you’re not trading your browsing data for that protection: Firefox doesn’t sell your browsing data, interrupt you with ads, or keep a record of the websites you visit. You can use VPN to: Keep the sites you visit private on shared Wi-Fi. You might use café Wi-Fi to check your itinerary, or look up something you’d prefer to keep to yourself while at a relative’s house. Turning on VPN helps hide the sites you’re visiting from whoever runs those Wi-Fi networks so your browsing habits stay your own. Change your browsing location. Firefox’s built-in VPN lets you change where your connection appears to come from, making it easy to check news from home while abroad. Two things to remember: VPN doesn’t make you anonymous online or hide browsing history on your device. Websites can recognize you through cookies or when you sign into an account. Use Private Window to browse without logging new visits in your Firefox history. Firefox’s built-in VPN only covers browsing within Firefox. For protection across other apps on your device, check out Mozilla VPN (a separate, paid subscription service). Firefox’s free built-in VPN is available to people using Firefox on desktop and Android (iOS is coming soon!). To start using the service: Sign up for a Mozilla account if you don’t yet have one. Select the VPN icon in Firefox’s toolbar on desktop or open the three-dot menu and go to Settings > VPN on your Android device. Follow the setup prompts, turn on VPN, and start browsing. You can check for availability in your region and review full instructions for using VPN on desktop and Android in our Help Center. Download Firefox to try it out today.   • Sign up for a Mozilla account if you don’t yet have one. 
  • Select the VPN icon in Firefox’s toolbar on desktop or open the three-dot menu and go to Settings > VPN on your Android device. 
  • Follow the setup prompts, turn on VPN, and start browsing. 

You can check for availability in your region and review full instructions for using VPN on desktop and Android in our Help Center.

Download Firefox to try it out today.

title: Five Firefox updates you might have missed, and a look ahead
text: Some of our latest Firefox updates have had big moments of their own, from the launch of our new design and built-in ad blocking on iOS to Firefox Enterprise and our partnership with NVIDIA GeForce NOW . You might’ve even spotted a few familiar internet OGs in our latest campaign . Other improvements might’ve flown under the radar until you open a PDF or move your tabs around. We wanted to take a moment to highlight some of the features and improvements we’ve been working on, from recent additions you might have missed to a look at what’s coming next . What’s new in Firefox Open PDFs faster. Firefox’s built-in PDF viewer now starts up to 45% faster on desktop, so there’s less waiting when you open a document in your browser. Put your Android tabs where you want them. Prefer your tabs at the bottom of the screen? You now have the option to move Firefox’s tab bar there. Go to Settings > Customize to choose. Find your spot in a video faster. We’ve made it quicker to jump to a different point in a video on desktop, whether you’re skipping ahead in a tutorial or going back to catch something you missed. Keep your favorite wallpapers handy. Firefox now saves a collection of your custom wallpapers under “Your images” on New Tab on desktop, so you can switch between favorites without uploading them again. Save time filling out forms and keeping up with page changes. Smart Window can now help fill out online forms using information from your chosen tabs, so you don’t have to copy details back and forth. You can also ask it to watch a page and notify you when something changes, like a price drop or a new job listing, saving you from manually checking for updates. Both capabilities are available in English in the U.S. and Canada as part of the Smart Window beta. Learn more about the new features here . What’s next on the Firefox roadmap When we launched our public roadmap in June, we shared plans to make everyday browsing more useful, flexible and private. We’ve now updated it with more of what’s ahead. We’re developing these features in the open, in close partnership with our contributors, and will share more about release timing as each feature gets ready for more people to try. Here’s a look at what’s in the works: Keep what you need in view. We heard your request for a way to keep a page visible while browsing. Mini Window will let you pop a tab, or part of a page, into a small floating window, so recipes or instructions stay in view while you work in another tab. Listen to pages. Give your eyes a break. Firefox will soon read articles and other web content aloud on desktop and Android, so you can listen while doing other things – even with your phone’s screen off. Take your reading offline. No connection? No problem. Offline mode on Android will let you save articles ahead of time to read or listen to without internet access, perfect for flights and commutes with spotty service. Turn speech into text on desktop. We’re bringing speech recognition to Firefox on desktop, so websites that use Firefox’s built-in capability can offer voice input and captions without sending your audio to a server. Those sites receive the text, while your audio stays on your device. After downloading the speech recognition model, transcription will work offline, too. Choose how VPN works for each site. Since bringing free built-in VPN to Firefox on desktop and Android (iOS coming soon), we’re now adding the ability to set website rules so you can choose how VPN works on a site-by-site basis. Clear browsing data directly from your toolbar. We’re bringing Private Window’s familiar button to Classic Window on desktop, so you can quickly choose what browsing data to delete without digging through settings. Keep shaping Firefox with us Try the latest updates and explore the Firefox roadmap for more of what we’re working on. If there’s something you’re looking forward to, or something you’d like us to improve, tell us on Mozilla Connect . Your feedback helps shape what comes next. The post Five Firefox updates you might have missed, and a look ahead appeared first on The Mozilla Blog .

Some of our latest Firefox updates have had big moments of their own, from the launch of our new design and built-in ad blocking on iOS to Firefox Enterprise and our partnership with NVIDIA GeForce NOW. You might’ve even spotted a few familiar internet OGs in our latest campaign. Other improvements might’ve flown under the radar until you open a PDF or move your tabs around.

We wanted to take a moment to highlight some of the features and improvements we’ve been working on, from recent additions you might have missed to a look at what’s coming next.

What’s new in Firefox

  1. Open PDFs faster. Firefox’s built-in PDF viewer now starts up to 45% faster on desktop, so there’s less waiting when you open a document in your browser.
  2. Put your Android tabs where you want them. Prefer your tabs at the bottom of the screen? You now have the option to move Firefox’s tab bar there. Go to Settings > Customize to choose.
  3. Find your spot in a video faster. We’ve made it quicker to jump to a different point in a video on desktop, whether you’re skipping ahead in a tutorial or going back to catch something you missed.
  4. Keep your favorite wallpapers handy. Firefox now saves a collection of your custom wallpapers under “Your images” on New Tab on desktop, so you can switch between favorites without uploading them again.
  5. Save time filling out forms and keeping up with page changes. Smart Window can now help fill out online forms using information from your chosen tabs, so you don’t have to copy details back and forth. You can also ask it to watch a page and notify you when something changes, like a price drop or a new job listing, saving you from manually checking for updates. Both capabilities are available in English in the U.S. and Canada as part of the Smart Window beta. Learn more about the new features here.

What’s next on the Firefox roadmap

When we launched our public roadmap in June, we shared plans to make everyday browsing more useful, flexible and private. We’ve now updated it with more of what’s ahead. We’re developing these features in the open, in close partnership with our contributors, and will share more about release timing as each feature gets ready for more people to try. 

Here’s a look at what’s in the works:

  • Keep what you need in view. We heard your request for a way to keep a page visible while browsing. Mini Window will let you pop a tab, or part of a page, into a small floating window, so recipes or instructions stay in view while you work in another tab.
  • Listen to pages. Give your eyes a break. Firefox will soon read articles and other web content aloud on desktop and Android, so you can listen while doing other things – even with your phone’s screen off. 
  • Take your reading offline. No connection? No problem. Offline mode on Android will let you save articles ahead of time to read or listen to without internet access, perfect for flights and commutes with spotty service.
  • Turn speech into text on desktop. We’re bringing speech recognition to Firefox on desktop, so websites that use Firefox’s built-in capability can offer voice input and captions without sending your audio to a server. Those sites receive the text, while your audio stays on your device. After downloading the speech recognition model, transcription will work offline, too.
  • Choose how VPN works for each site. Since bringing free built-in VPN to Firefox on desktop and Android (iOS coming soon), we’re now adding the ability to set website rules so you can choose how VPN works on a site-by-site basis.
  • Clear browsing data directly from your toolbar. We’re bringing Private Window’s familiar button to Classic Window on desktop, so you can quickly choose what browsing data to delete without digging through settings.

Keep shaping Firefox with us

Try the latest updates and explore the Firefox roadmap for more of what we’re working on. If there’s something you’re looking forward to, or something you’d like us to improve, tell us on Mozilla Connect. Your feedback helps shape what comes next.

The post Five Firefox updates you might have missed, and a look ahead appeared first on The Mozilla Blog.

title: Skip the busywork with Smart Window
text: The days might be getting shorter, but your to-do list is only getting longer. Whether you’re getting a head start on holiday shopping or planning your next career move, Smart Window’s newest features will help you keep up. Firefox’s opt-in AI browsing experience can now use information from tabs you choose to help fill out forms. It can also watch web pages and notify you about specific changes you’ve asked it to track. Let your open tabs fill in the blanks Job applications ask for your work history; event registrations ask for a professional bio. If those details are already in your open tabs, Smart Window can now use pages you choose to suggest what to enter, saving you extra clicks and some Ctrl+C, Ctrl+V. For example, Smart Window could use information from your online portfolio or professional profile to fill in your work history, or draw on those details to draft an answer to a question like “Tell me about a time when…” Firefox’s regular autofill still handles saved information such as your name and address, which can be entered directly into forms without relying on AI models. To get started, click into a form field. If the form has at least four text fields that Smart Window can help fill, you’ll see “Fill from sources” appear in the dropdown, along with a recommended source page. Select “Fill from sources” to continue, or click the pencil icon to open “Edit sources” if you want to change or add tabs. Once you’ve chosen your sources, review the suggestions before filling out the form. You can edit the results before submitting; Smart Window won’t submit the form for you. When you choose to use this feature, information from your selected source pages is shared with Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite, the AI model used for detecting the fields and extracting relevant information from your selected tabs. Your model choice for Smart Window chat stays the same, and saved autofill values stay on your device. Learn more about how form filling works . This feature currently supports text fields on web forms and does not save any generated form fill data. We’re exploring support for more field types, including dropdown menus, as well as PDF forms and ways to save and manage generated information for future forms. Give your refresh button a break A watched pot never boils, and refreshing a web page won’t make an update appear any sooner. Smart Window can now watch a page for a specific update, whether that’s an item going on sale or a new job listing that includes a job title or company name that you’re following. Each task can follow up to five pages, so you can keep an eye on several stores or job boards at the same time. Type “/watch” in the Smart Window chat to set up a task. Describe what you’re looking for, add the pages to watch, and choose whether Firefox should check for updates on a daily or weekly basis. Those checks run only while the browser is open. When there’s a match, you’ll see an update through the Tasks button in the toolbar. With desktop notifications enabled, Firefox can also notify you directly; click the notification to open the watched pages. You can have up to 15 active tasks at a time, and you can edit, pause or delete tasks. Smart Window will automatically pause tasks after 60 days without a matching change. If 90 days pass without a change, it will stop checking altogether. Page monitoring uses the Qwen AI model to identify changes that match what you’re looking for. Your model choice for Smart Window chat stays the same. Learn more about creating and managing tasks . Try the latest additions These two new features are available in the Smart Window beta on desktop, in English in the U.S. and Canada, and will roll out to additional markets in the coming months. Try Smart Window and share your experience on Mozilla Connect . We’d love to hear how you’re using Smart Window to get things done and what you’d like it to help with next. With desktop notifications enabled, Firefox can also notify you directly; click the notification to open the watched pages. You can have up to 15 active tasks at a time, and you can edit, pause or delete tasks. Smart Window will automatically pause tasks after 60 days without a matching change. If 90 days pass without a change, it will stop checking altogether. 

Page monitoring uses the Qwen AI model to identify changes that match what you’re looking for. Your model choice for Smart Window chat stays the same. Learn more about creating and managing tasks.

Try the latest additions

These two new features are available in the Smart Window beta on desktop, in English in the U.S. and Canada, and will roll out to additional markets in the coming months.

Try Smart Window and share your experience on Mozilla Connect. We’d love to hear how you’re using Smart Window to get things done and what you’d like it to help with next.

title: Still here, still yours: 5 reasons to choose Firefox
text: The internet used to feel like a community, not a commodity. Browsers were tools for exploration, and you could wander the web without feeling tracked everywhere. Today, as the web becomes increasingly surveilled and commercialized, Firefox preserves the magic, freedom, and fun of the early internet. Still open source, still independent, still privacy-focused. No billionaire owner, no hidden agenda. So, whether you’re new here, back after a break, or just curious, here are five reasons to choose the browser that puts you first. Backed by a non-profit, not billionaires Firefox is backed by the Mozilla Foundation, a non-profit committed to an open internet. Unlike other big tech companies, we’re built with privacy as the default . Our open source code is visible, reviewable, and continuously stress-tested by a global community, truly putting power in the hands of the people it’s built for. Private and fast by design While other browsers allow third-party trackers to profile you, Firefox’s Enhanced Tracking Protection (ETP) helps stop cross-site tracking before it starts, letting your browser work faster. Plus, when you sync information like history and bookmarks across devices, it’s encrypted locally, meaning only you can access it. Learn about some of our other privacy-focused features like password manager , built-in VPN , and Relay in our guide to strengthening your online security for free with Firefox . AI on your terms We believe the only person who should decide how you interact with AI features in your browser is you. Firefox offers a clear, easily accessible AI controls section where you can turn off AI features entirely — or decide which ones stay on depending on your workflow and preferences. For those wanting a little more help getting things done, Smart Window is Firefox’s most integrated AI experience. With your permission, its built-in, AI-powered assistant can work directly with your open tabs and browsing history to connect the dots. This means it can compare information, summarize pages, and help plan projects without requiring you to provide context from your past and current browsing activity every time you start a new prompt. Newer feature additions to Smart Window include the ability to group related tabs together and visual history previews that help you find a page you visited earlier when you can’t remember the exact URL or phrase searched. Also, our partnership with Exa enables Smart Window to find current web information to include in responses while also displaying the sources behind these answers, so you can verify what you’re seeing without interrupting your workflow. Smart Window remains in beta as we continue to learn and improve from our community’s feedback. Try it yourself here . Not just Chrome in disguise Firefox is not built on Chromium, the open source browser project that supports Google Chrome and many other browsers. As a matter of fact, we are one of the last major browsers that isn’t. Instead, Firefox runs on Mozilla’s independent Gecko browser engine, which was developed specifically to uphold our strong privacy standards and give people more control over their data and browsing experience. This independence also impacts how Firefox handles browser add-ons , particularly ad blockers. Unlike Chromium-based browsers that now limit how powerful ad-blocking tools can be, Firefox still allows ad blockers like uBlock Origin to work at full strength. This means people who use Firefox can enjoy stronger, more reliable ad and tracker blocking without compromise, something increasingly difficult on Chromium-based browsers due to imposed limitations. Plus, we have a really cute Firefox Firefox is constantly building features and solutions to help you navigate the web on your own terms, and we wanted to make this support visible. Enter Kit , Firefox’s companion to the internet. Kit isn’t an AI assistant or chatbot, just a friendly face that you might see during moments that are meant to feel friendly and supportive, like when you’re just getting set up, exploring a new feature, or celebrating a win such as successfully adjusting a setting. Rooted in values, built for you While the internet is ever-changing, Firefox remains rooted in the values that defined its beginning. Our browser was created on the principles of privacy, independence, and choice,and we continue to uphold them as we innovate and evolve. In a web landscape dominated by profit, surveillance, and sameness, our browser preserves the open and human spirit of the early internet. New, returning, or loyal for years, there’s always a place for you here. Download Firefox and make the web yours again. title: Why is the CMA asking us to choose the furniture before the house? The UK’s search choice screens need browser choice screens alongside them
text: Mobile browsers are a key gateway to the internet for 56 million people in the UK. Smartphone users spend around half an hour a day in these apps, and opening a browser is the most common way they look up information online. Yet most people are using a smartphone browser that was preinstalled and set as the default for them, without ever being asked which browser they would actually prefer. Mozilla believes people deserve an active choice in the tools they depend on every day, which is why the latest proposals from the UK Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) matter. We welcome the CMA’s plans to give people a choice of search service and are asking it to consult on browser choice now, so both screens can launch together. On September 23rd, the CMA published updated plans that would require Google to show people in the UK a choice of search service on new Android devices, covering the default search app and home-screen search widget as well as Chrome. Search choice screens would also appear in Chrome on other platforms, including through a major update for existing users. Some AI assistants would also be eligible to appear alongside search engines. The proposals are well designed, but solve only half the problem The CMA’s mobile browser investigation found that preinstallation, prominent placement and default settings restrict browser competition. Mozilla’s innovative 2023 experiment showed that properly designed browser choice screens can help people choose a browser they expect to keep using, and can be an effective tool for giving people agency over their online life. It also showed that an overwhelming majority of people (98%!) want to see them. The EU Digital Markets Act has since demonstrated their impact in practice. We welcome the CMA’s work on search choice, but people in the UK deserve browser choice too. Asking people to pick a search service inside a browser that most of them never actively chose in the first place leaves some of the biggest issues identified in the CMA’s own mobile browser investigation unaddressed. The CMA commissioned user research on search choice screens to refine and improve the proposals it first consulted on in January. Providers’ positions on the choice screen would be fully randomised. Users would have to scroll to the bottom before confirming, and could “test drive” a search provider for at least a week. The CMA has also recognized that search is changing. Its research found that many people were already using AI assistants to search alongside traditional search services. Under the revised, more technology-neutral eligibility criteria, an AI assistant could also qualify to appear on the search choice screen if it meets the requirements, including being able to search the web and attribute its sources. But browser choice should not be left behind. Why the two choices belong together Less confusion. The CMA’s new research found that participants often confused browsers with search services and were unsure what their search choice would change. Mozilla’s research has revealed similar confusion. These findings support designing and testing the two screens together, with clear explanations of each decision. Less duplication. The CMA’s work on search choice can also inform browser choice. Developing the two together would allow the design, order and timing to be tested as one journey, helping to avoid separate rounds of changes and interruptions for users. Order matters. Nobody chooses the furniture before the house. Browsers have their own search defaults, which is why we recommend showing the browser choice screen first, followed by the search screen, with wording that makes clear these are two separate decisions. The EU and Japan already show both screens The EU’s Digital Markets Act introduced browser choice screens on iOS for the first time and brought browser and search choice together during Android set-up. Browser first, then search, so the relationship between the two makes sense. In Japan, search and browser choice screens are presented on both Android and iOS. And people are making use of the browser screen to select alternatives. In May, we reported Firefox is selected through a DMA choice screen once every ten seconds , with retention five times higher than for organic downloads. Other independent browsers have also reported substantial growth. Choice matters more as AI moves into the browser The CMA’s proposals recognize that AI is changing how people search. AI is also changing what browsers offer, adding to the ways they compete on features, privacy and user control. Firefox already lets people on desktop pick which AI assistant sits in the sidebar , and our Smart Window beta extends that choice to the model behind the browser’s own assistant. There are meaningful differences between browsers. AI is the latest example of why giving people an active choice matters. When people aren’t offered an active browser choice, they may be choosing search and AI services within a browser someone else picked. One decision taken at the factory can end up shaping the ones that follow. A search choice screen gives people a say over their search provider; offering browser choice alongside it would give them a say over that first decision too. Our ask of the CMA We’re asking the CMA to consult now on browser choice screens for Apple’s and Google’s mobile platforms, so they can launch alongside the search screens. Apple and Google already offer browser choice screens in the EU and Japan. The CMA can draw on that experience and its own research to give people in the UK an active choice of both browser and search service. Mozilla’s response to the consultation is available here . Firefox already lets people on desktop pick which AI assistant sits in the sidebar, and our Smart Window beta extends that choice to the model behind the browser’s own assistant. There are meaningful differences between browsers. AI is the latest example of why giving people an active choice matters.

When people aren’t offered an active browser choice, they may be choosing search and AI services within a browser someone else picked. One decision taken at the factory can end up shaping the ones that follow. A search choice screen gives people a say over their search provider; offering browser choice alongside it would give them a say over that first decision too.

Our ask of the CMA

We’re asking the CMA to consult now on browser choice screens for Apple’s and Google’s mobile platforms, so they can launch alongside the search screens. Apple and Google already offer browser choice screens in the EU and Japan. The CMA can draw on that experience and its own research to give people in the UK an active choice of both browser and search service.

title: This map shows the most important asset that VC-backed companies need right now
text: What’s the most vital asset for an AI company today? For venture backed AI business, it might be “funding” or “revenue”. But, there’s another asset that’s just as critical: trust . At Mozilla, building technology that people and businesses can genuinely trust has been a long-standing, guiding principle . That’s why we’re supporting the launch of the Trustworthy AI Map , a market map of VC-backed companies building the infrastructure for trustworthy AI. Supported by seven organizations, including Mozilla, the Trustworthy AI Map features 79 companies across 15 countries, from early to later-stage venture. It maps companies building products for AI deployment across seven layers of the AI stack, including identity, data control, interoperability and evaluation. The map connects the products with the companies and capital behind them, helping investors, founders and businesses explore commercial opportunities. To be featured, trust must be baked into its product or business model through human agency, trust by design or aligned business models. This initiative aligns with much of our work over the past year. We’ve invested in companies through Mozilla Ventures, launched Otari, an open source enterprise tool which allows you to control your LLM infrastructure from a single layer, and published landmark research in our State of Open Source AI report that’s demystifying the open source AI landscape and shows that the capability gap between open and closed models is closing. We’ve also partnered with Mila: the Quebec AI Institute, to build an open source AI foundation layer that enables organizations and institutions to own and operate their own advanced AI systems locally, ensuring full control over their technology and data. The project has the backing of the Canadian government, and industry leaders like Hypertec. At a time when fear and uncertainty about AI are on the rise, trust is not just a virtue; it’s a path towards profitability. Explore the Trustworthy AI Map to see how. Learn more at trustworthyaimap.org . The post This map shows the most important asset that VC-backed companies need right now appeared first on The Mozilla Blog .
